1	---
2	name: verify-in-production
3	description: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
4	---
5	
6	# Verify in production
7	
8	A change is finished when someone has watched it work. Most changes you can watch **now**, and
9	that is the rule — this skill is only for the rest: a change whose proof lives somewhere the
10	repo cannot see yet. You are filing the proof, not doing the work — and the proof itself runs
11	unattended: an automatic check, end to end, with a person entering
12	only where no automatic check can exist.
13	
14	## When it fires: after the merge, never before
15	
16	**The PR must have merged.** This skill runs as a step of the merge, unasked — `merge-to-main`
17	calls it once the squash has landed — and at no other moment. Not when the code is written, not
18	when the PR opens, not while review is in flight.
19	
20	The reason is that a PR can be **rejected**, and a branch that is still open can be rewritten
21	under you. Both leave a verification whose premise never reached `main`:
22	
23	- A **rewritten branch** makes the brief describe a change that no longer exists. #1121 was filed
24	  against a scope its PR then dropped; the verification was moot before the merge it waited on.
25	- A **rejected PR** is worse, because the queue cannot tell it from a merge. A blocked item
26	  releases on its blocker being *closed*, and nothing reads `merged` — so the item goes ready,
27	  reads an `In-production-when:` that can never become true, pushes `Not-before:` forward by
28	  `Retry-every:` without comment, and repeats indefinitely. No janitor rule reclaims it: the
29	  stale-ready sweep cannot see an item sleeping on a future `Not-before`, and the
30	  stuck-dependency sweep exempts an item whose blockers have closed.
31	
32	So there is no such thing as filing this early and letting the queue sort it out. Wait for the
33	merge, then read **what actually landed** — the merged diff, not the branch you remember writing.
34	
35	## First: does this file anything at all?
36	
37	Most changes **file nothing.** Run the test in this order and stop at the first answer:
38	
39	1. **Did you watch it work in this session?** Then it is proven. File nothing.
40	2. **Did a test that ran prove it?** A unit test, a CI job, an executable-requirements or UI
41	   test covering exactly the behaviour that changed. File nothing — the suite is the mechanism
42	   that comes back.
43	3. **Does the change have an observable effect at all?** A comment, a design doc, a README, a
44	   rename with no behavioural edge, a refactor a passing suite already pins. File nothing.
45	4. **Otherwise: where does its effect first become observable?** If the answer is a place and a
46	   moment — a member repo once it converges, a site once it deploys, a session once it reloads
47	   its rules — that is what you file.
48	
49	The bar is *could not be watched now*, not *would be nice to double-check*. A verification
50	filed for a change already covered by a test is a wasted run re-proving what the suite proved.
51	
52	## What you file
53	
54	**A deferred request** — the same ad-hoc lane `/do-later` rides, so the queue does the waiting,
55	the running and the lifecycle; nothing here adds machinery beside it. One issue, titled
56	`Verify in production: <the change, in a few words>`, its body the whole brief: the run that
57	verifies will never see this conversation and may be days away. Say what changed and why it
58	could not be watched now, then, each spelled verbatim on its own line:
59	
60	```
61	Original-issue: #<the change's issue>
62	In-production-when: <the concrete artifact to read, and what makes it true>
63	Verify: <what to observe, and what counts as a pass>
64	Not-before: <ISO instant just past the expected release>
65	Retry-every: <how far to push Not-before when not yet live, e.g. 1 day>
66	```
67	
68	No `Blocked-by:`. You are filing after the merge, so the change's PR has already closed and
69	there is nothing left to wait on but the release itself.
70	
71	- **`Original-issue:`** is where a failure lands — the issue the change was done under, which
72	  the run reopens if the verification fails. Make the verification that issue's **sub-issue**
73	  too (`mcp__github__sub_issue_write`, method `add`, `issue_number` the original,
74	  `sub_issue_id` the **id** the create call returned, not its number), so the change it proves
75	  shows what is still unproven about it — [RULES.md](../../RULES.md)' *Filing an issue that
76	  belongs under another*, applied where there is no PR left to carry the link.
77	- **`In-production-when:`** names a thing to *read*, never a duration to wait. "`missingbulb/Shepherd`'s
78	  `.claudinite-settings.json` stamps `packVersions.tidy-repo` at 8 or higher." "The live site's
79	  `/version.json` reports a version past 4.2.0." "Any session started after this landed — check
80	  the vendored copy under `.claudinite/shared/` carries the new text." A merge is not a
81	  production condition, and neither is elapsed time.
82	- **`Verify:`** is an assertion with a pass condition, not a topic — and a read an **unattended
83	  run can make**: an API response, a file at a URL, an issue's state. "Issue #100 on that repo
84	  is closed with a comment citing the scheduler runs" beats "check tidy-issues works". Only where no
85	  automatic check can exist may `Verify:` name a person's step, spelled out exactly.
86	- **`Not-before:`** is the queue's own wait field: adoption holds the run until the moment has
87	  passed. Aim it just past the release you expect — the re-arm covers a miss, so don't pad it.
88	- **`Retry-every:`** is the extension you are prescribing: when the run finds the change not
89	  yet live, it pushes `Not-before:` forward by exactly this much. Size it to the release you
90	  wait on — a nightly converge retries daily, a next-session rule in minutes.
91	
92	Then the mark, as `/do-later` applies it: **`task:origin:ad-hoc`**, the one label the scheduler
93	run adopts. Beside it, in the body, **`Model: sonnet`** (reading a live artifact and judging an
94	assertion against it). Never `Automerge:` — a verification has nothing to merge. If the mark
95	doesn't exist in the repo yet, say so and leave the issue — it appears on the next scheduler run.
96	
97	## Tell the run how to converge
98	
99	End the body with instructions to the run itself — the issue is its whole brief, and the run
100	decides nothing: it executes this playbook.
101	
102	1. Read `In-production-when:` against the real artifact. Never infer it from a merge, a green
103	   run, or elapsed time.
104	2. **Live** → run `Verify:`. Passes: comment the evidence actually read (the version, the value,
105	   the URL) and close this issue as completed. Fails: reopen `Original-issue:` with a comment
106	   saying what was asserted, what happened instead and where you read it; comment here linking
107	   that; close this issue as completed — the verification did its job by finding the fault.
108	3. **Not yet live** → push `Not-before:` forward by `Retry-every:`, **clear the issue's
109	   `task:status:*` label** (clearing the status is the whole of the re-ask — the mark stays on
110	   for life), and leave the issue open. The next scheduler run re-adopts it, and the bumped
111	   field holds it until the new moment. No comment; the bumped field is the record.
112	
113	## Then say what you filed
114	
115	One line back to the owner: the issue link, what it waits on, and its retry cadence.
116

1	---
2	name: writing-migration-plans
3	description: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
4	---
5	
6	# Writing migration and implementation plans
7	
8	A plan's phases are not a narrative of the work; they are a **schedule of who has to be present
9	when**. Ordering them by topic — "phase 1: the store, phase 2: the workers, phase 3: cutover" —
10	scatters the moments that need a human across the whole run, and every one of them stops it. Order
11	them by *what blocks*, and the run ends with a stretch nobody has to attend.
12	
13	The shape this produces, in one line: **setup, then one approval of everything, then a chain that
14	runs itself.** All the code is written before the owner is asked for anything — the cleanup and
15	the destructive tail included — so their attention is spent once; and every step after that
16	approval is a queued continuation armed on the step before it, so the migration advances without
17	anyone remembering it exists.
18	
19	Everything below assumes the change is already agreed: the problem, and that this migration is the
20	right way to solve it (basics' *Starting any requested change*). The end-state's **shape** —
21	converging in one forced pass, accepting legacy input at the door, a standing mechanism for
22	stragglers — is [RULES.md](../../RULES.md)' *Planning a migration*; this skill is the ordering.
23	
24	## Two deliverables, two homes — and only two
25	
26	An initiative produces at most one document and one issue, and neither may do the
27	other's job:
28	
29	- **The design doc** (`docs/<initiative>/DESIGN.md`, where the project keeps one)
30	  describes the **end state and its rationale** — what the mechanism is once the
31	  work is done, and why that shape over the alternatives, with each alternative's
32	  drawbacks stated. It never carries the previous state as narrative, the requests
33	  or conversation that led here, owner attributions or opinions, progress, or a
34	  phase list. The test: a reader who arrives after the migration finishes must
35	  find nothing to delete. Legacy shapes appear only where the end state itself
36	  keeps handling them (a decode map, an accepted input) — as mechanism, not as
37	  history.
38	- **The migration is work, not a document.** Its plan lives in the tracking issue
39	  and nowhere else — never a plan or migration document committed to the repo. A
40	  plan document goes stale the moment work starts and cannot be checked off; the
41	  issue is checkable, append-only, and dies with the work.
42	
43	## The three blocks, and where each belongs
44	
45	Sort every step of the plan into one of three kinds, and let that sort — not the subject matter —
46	decide the phase it lands in.
47	
48	**1. Out-of-band setup — before any code changes.** Anything performed outside the repo that a
49	later step will need: provisioning an environment, creating a session or runner, setting a secret
50	or variable, granting a permission, flipping a platform setting, registering a webhook. Nearly all
51	of it is **non-destructive** — it adds a capability that nothing yet consumes, so doing it early
52	costs nothing and changes no behaviour. Doing it *late* costs the whole run: the plan reaches the
53	step that reads the secret and stops until someone is available.
54	
55	Front-load all of it into phase zero, before the first line of code. Write it as its own issue
56	with a checkbox per step (basics' *Handing over a human-only step*), stating for each what stays
57	broken while it is off. And before writing it down, confirm you genuinely cannot do it yourself —
58	a step handed to a human that you could have taken is the most expensive kind of block there is.
59	
60	The exception is the genuinely destructive step — deleting the old store, revoking the old
61	credential, removing the compatibility shim. Those are not setup; they are the migration's tail,
62	and they belong after the cutover has been observed working — which is **not** a later phase. A
63	cleanup phase falls due long after the run that would have done it ended, and nothing brings it
64	back.
65	
66	**Write its code anyway, now, in the stack** (the next sort), so the owner approves it with
67	everything else — and make its *merge* a link in the chain below, armed on the cutover being
68	observed. What must never be deferred is the writing and the approving; what must always be
69	deferred is the merging.
70	
71	**2. Review and authorization gates — collapsed into one pass.** Every phase that ships code is a
72	gate: the owner must read it and approve it before the next phase can start. A plan with four
73	coding phases has four such waits, and each one is dead time whose length nobody controls.
74	
75	Write **all** the code first — every phase of it, including the cleanup and the destructive tail —
76	as a stack of PRs each based on the previous, and put the whole stack in front of the owner
77	together. The stack keeps the reviewable units small and independent — one concern per PR, as ever
78	— while costing one arrival of attention rather than four.
79	
80	*Write* is not *merge*. A PR whose merge must wait on something being observed still gets written,
81	reviewed and approved in this pass; what waits is its merge, and the thing that performs that
82	merge is a link in the chain (below), not a person's memory. Say so in that PR's body: what gates
83	it, and which queued step will merge it.
84	
85	Approval of the stack is approval of the stack: it does not extend to a fix authored afterwards
86	(basics' *Acting on an approval to merge, ship or proceed*).
87	
88	**3. Execution steps — a chain, not a checklist.** Once phase zero has landed the setup and the
89	approved stack has begun merging, the remaining steps run the migration: force the converge,
90	backfill the members, watch the cutover, merge the gated PR, retire the shim. If the first two
91	sorts were done properly there is no *approval* gate among them — but there is almost always a
92	**wait**, because each step's precondition is the previous step's effect becoming observable
93	somewhere the repo cannot see yet.
94	
95	A wait is not a reason to write "then, later, do X". Every one of these steps is filed, at plan
96	time, as a queued continuation armed on the step before it. See **The chain** below.
97	
98	That is the test of the plan. **Read the phases in order and mark every point where the run would
99	have to stop and wait for a person.** Each mark that falls after phase zero and the review pass is
100	a step that was sorted wrong — or a step that should have been a link in the chain and was written
101	as a note instead. Move it, chain it, or say in the plan why it genuinely cannot be either.
102	
103	## The chain
104	
105	Everything after the approval is a run that arms the next run. The mechanism is the queue's own
106	ad-hoc lane — the one `/do-later` and `verify-in-production` file into — and nothing here adds
107	machinery beside it: an ordinary issue, marked for the queue, carrying its own brief.
108	
109	**File the whole chain when the plan is agreed**, not as each step falls due. One issue per
110	execution step, each naming the previous in `Blocked-by:`, so the queue does the waiting: a
111	blocked item is released when its blocker closes, which is exactly "the step before it finished".
112	Filing the chain up front is what makes it a mechanism rather than a habit — a chain that depends
113	on each run remembering to file its successor breaks silently the first time a run parks.
114	
115	Each link is a **sub-issue of the tracking issue** ([RULES.md](../../RULES.md)' *Filing an issue
116	that belongs under another*), so the plan and its chain are one hierarchy read two ways rather
117	than two lists that can disagree. Where a link is a PR's merge rather than a run, that PR's body
118	closes **the link**, never the tracker: a phase PR carrying `Closes #<tracker>` ends the whole
119	migration on its first merge.
120	
121	Each link's body is its whole brief, because the run that picks it up will never see the
122	conversation that planned it. Four things, and the first two are what make the link *chainable*:
123	
124	- **What makes this step's world ready** — a thing to *read*, never a duration: a stamp, a file at
125	  a URL, an API answer. (`verify-in-production` spells this as `In-production-when:`, and a link
126	  that waits on a release rather than on the previous issue closing rides `Not-before:` +
127	  `Retry-every:` instead of `Blocked-by:`.)
128	- **What counts as this step having worked** — the assertion its own successor is waiting on.
129	  This is the load-bearing half: the chain advances on *validation*, not on the step having run.
130	- **The playbook**, exact enough to execute without judgment: what to do, and what to do when the
131	  check fails (comment what was read, leave the issue open — a failed step must not close, because
132	  closing is what releases the next link).
133	- **How it ends**: comment the evidence on the tracking issue, then close as completed. That close
134	  is the trigger for the next link, so it happens last and only on success.
135	
136	Three hazards worth stating once:
137	
138	- **Closing is the trigger, and nothing distinguishes a `completed` close from a `not planned`
139	  one.** Abandoning the migration means closing the *rest* of the chain first, tail-first; closing
140	  a link to tidy it away releases its successor into a world that is not ready.
141	- **A link that cannot make its reads must park, not guess.** A rate-limited or scope-blocked
142	  sweep answers "all clear" in exactly the way a healthy fleet does.
143	- **A chain is only as visible as its tracking issue.** Every link comments its result there, so
144	  the plan's checkboxes and the chain's state never have to be reconciled by hand.
145	
146	## Writing it down
147	
148	- **The plan is a tracking issue**, and the phases are its checkboxes. Status and remaining work
149	  live there; a design document, where the project keeps one, carries the mechanism and not the
150	  progress.
151	- **Each phase names its exit condition**, observable and stated as a thing that reads back true —
152	  not "cutover done" but "every member's stamp shows the new ref". A phase whose end is a judgment
153	  call is a phase that stays open.
154	- **Nothing closes on a human's memory.** A step you cannot verify now gets a mechanism that comes
155	  to you — a link in the chain, a scheduled task, an issue something converges (basics' *When
156	  verifying now is genuinely impossible*). A phase whose closing condition is "check next week" is
157	  not a phase.
158	- **Every execution phase names its link.** The checkbox says which issue runs it, so the plan and
159	  the queue are one thing read two ways rather than two lists that can disagree.
160	- **Size each step to what it is**, and don't restate in the plan what the design document or the
161	  linked issue already carries.
162	
163	## Working through the plan
164	
165	Once the plan is agreed, the issue body's plan is **append-only**. While implementing, scheduler run its
166	checkboxes and add below it — a comment, or a new section for what the work turned up — and never
167	edit, reword, condense or re-order what was already there.
168	
169	The body is the record of what was agreed, and it is the only copy: an edit overwrites it in place
170	with nothing left to diff against, so a plan silently rewritten to match what was built reads
171	afterwards as a plan that was followed. Keeping it fixed is what makes the divergence visible —
172	and a divergence is the interesting part, not an embarrassment to tidy away.
173	
174	So when the work shows a phase was wrong, say so **underneath**: what the plan assumed, what turned
175	out to be true, and what you did instead. If that changes the plan going forward, the new steps are
176	an addition, appended and dated; the superseded ones stay where they are, marked superseded rather
177	than deleted.
178	
179	The exception is a **correction to the plan itself before implementation of it starts** — the owner
180	saying the plan misreads what they asked for. That is a correction (basics' *Acting on a
181	correction*): repair the body, since there is no work yet for it to have diverged from.
182	
183	## Reviewing someone else's plan
184	
185	Run the same sort over it. The findings worth raising, in order of what they cost:
186	
187	1. A secret, permission, environment or account created **after** code that depends on it.
188	2. More than one review gate — two or more phases that each end in "open a PR and wait".
189	3. Code left unwritten because its phase is "later" — the cleanup and the destructive tail
190	   above all. Everything the migration will need is written and approved in the one pass; only
191	   merges and effects are deferred.
192	4. An execution step written as a note rather than filed as a link — anything phrased "then,
193	   once X, do Y" with no issue that comes back when X.
194	5. A chain whose links advance on a step having *run* rather than on its result being *read*.
195	6. A destructive step scheduled before the replacement has been observed working.
196	7. A phase with no stated exit condition, or one only a person can judge.
197	8. A step handed to a human that the agent could have performed itself.
198

1	---
2	name: writing-tests
3	description: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
4	---
5	
6	# Testing practices
7	
8	Portable practices for writing tests you can actually trust — proving a test fails before relying on it, snapshot/golden discipline, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, and how to gate a fuzzy quality metric. These are project-agnostic; a consuming repo's own test *mechanics* (runner, layout, which suites exist) stay in its own docs. (General software-engineering practices live in [the basics pack's RULES.md](../../RULES.md); CI-trigger rules and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` workflow-recursion gotcha live in [the git-github-advanced skill](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md).)
9	
10	- See a test fail before you trust it: write it red before the fix (green after), or break what it guards and watch it go red. A test that has never failed proves nothing. For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. See-it-fail there **must** be the second method — mutate the new guard (weaken it), watch the test bite, then restore it. Restore with `git checkout -- <file>` (or `git stash`) taken at the moment of mutating — never a `.bak` copy saved earlier, which predates whatever else you edited in between and silently discards that intervening work.
11	- A mechanism meant to survive a retry, re-queue, or hand-off needs a test that calls it twice, not once. A suite of single-call tests stays green while the multi-call case corrupts state — the double-call is what a real retry, requeue, or hand-off actually does. When the mechanism arbitrates by identity (a claim, a lock), the second call must come from a **different actor**: a single actor retrying its own stale claim can't expose an identity-masked race, since it still recognizes its own claim as valid.
12	- A simulator of a stateful mechanism must advance state only where the real engine's code actually leaves a mark — never wherever the rule's stated description says a transition happens. A sim that fires on every event matching the rule's *intent* is correct by construction against that rule and blind to exactly the silent paths where the real implementation and the rule have quietly diverged — which is where a genuine bug usually lives. Read the real engine's code for what it *writes*, and model that.
13	- Before trusting a new transform/normalizer, run it over the *real existing corpus* it will process, not just hand-picked test inputs — the live data exposes edge cases your examples won't. (A hostname-apex helper passed its tests but mis-stripped `tel-aviv.gov.il` → `gov.il`; the gap only surfaced when the function was run over the actual list of existing URLs.) Relatedly, prefer a generic structural rule over a hand-maintained list of special cases: the enumerated list needs per-instance upkeep and silently has gaps, while a rule keyed on structure (e.g. "a known registry label under any 2-letter ccTLD") covers the whole class at once.
14	- A test that stubs the exact boundary where the bug lives can't catch that bug — it guards only the shape it asserts, not the runtime effect. Say what it can't catch.
15	- A test that dereferences a path inside a **read-only dependency tree someone else refreshes** — a vendored mount, a synced submodule, generated output from an upstream build — is a test whose fixture a stranger can delete: the day upstream retires that file the case fails `ENOENT` with nothing in your repo having changed. Assert against a path only when the test itself creates it; when a case genuinely needs an upstream file, read it **defensively** and skip with a stated reason if it is gone, so a retirement upstream reports as "no longer applicable" rather than as your repo being broken. Check what actually runs these cases too — a suite that the repo's own gate never invokes reports its breakage to whoever happens to look.
16	- **Never pin a declaration to itself.** Asserting that a config/manifest field equals the literal it is declared with (`assert.equal(task.expected_outcome, 'open-pr')`, `assert.equal(pack.id, 'thing')`) restates the file under test in a second file. It can only fail when someone changes the value **on purpose**, so it catches no defect and instead taxes every deliberate change with a mirrored edit — and, worse, teaches that the value is load-bearing prose to be restated, which is how one setting ends up copied into a comment, a worker doc, a README table and a test, so flipping it becomes a five-file diff. The see-it-fail test exposes it: to make the assertion go red you must break the thing it asserts, which is not a bug. Assert what can actually come apart — a claim spanning two artifacts that could drift independently: the doc a field *names* exists; every signal the code reads is declared; two implementations of the same list agree; a value the runtime constrains is inside its legal set. If a declaration genuinely must not change without deliberation, that is a review concern, not a test.
17	- Prefer a single shared double; but when a subsystem is faked by more than one (a minimal unit stub vs. a faithful harness that boots the real module), a new call into the faked surface must be taught to **every** double, or the untaught one breaks — and the faithful harness turns an unmodeled API into a confusing **far-away** failure (a DOM-snapshot pixel-diff, not a local error at the call site). After adding a call into a faked boundary, find every double of it and extend each.
18	- When one wire format, encoding, or algorithm is **implemented twice** — two languages, two tiers, a hand-rolled client encoder against the server's library — no compiler, type system, or single test run spans the two, so the only thing holding them together is a **shared vector set carried deliberately by both suites**: the same inputs and the same expected outputs, asserted independently on each side, including the boundary cases the two could plausibly round differently (a value exactly on a bisection midpoint, a tie, a truncation edge). A vector asserted on only one side is an input nobody ever compared — both suites stay green, in different languages under different runners, while the claim quietly stops covering it. So: touching *either* implementation re-runs *both* suites, and adding a vector adds it to both. Where the pairing is mechanical (the two vector lists must contain the same inputs), pin it with a check rather than a convention.
19	- A traceability/coverage gate that requires every spec item be *claimed* by some test of one fixed kind proves only that it's claimed, not that it's verified. When items differ in kind, the gate green-lights claims that kind can't check — a pixel snapshot "covers" a click's tab-opening it can never observe, or a state the case never renders (and can't, when the data can't reach it). Segment the gate by the verification each item needs (route behavior to a behavior test, rendering to a snapshot) rather than forcing every item onto one mechanism. (A UI-snapshot coverage gate parked behavioral leaves `9.1`–`9.3`/`3.4` and an unreachable `8.6` on cases that render none of them — issue #429.)
20	- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
21	- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). Thread the reference time through the code under test, defaulting to the real clock in production. When retrofitting such a rule into an existing fixture suite, pin the reference instant so existing fixtures land on the same side they were authored for — so only the cases that deliberately exercise the new rule change and the diff stays small and reviewable, rather than a sprawling baseline churn that buries the intended change.
22	- A round-trip test that asserts by comparing **serialized** forms (`JSON.stringify(decoded) === JSON.stringify(original)`) silently makes key *order* part of the contract: add a field at the top of the encoder's record and append it in the decoder's, and the round-trip fails on ordering alone — with a diff that reads like a data bug and sends you after a value that was correct all along. Deep-equal the parsed structures instead, so the test states what it means; keep serialized comparison only where byte-identity is genuinely the property under test, and say so in the test.
23	- A new **e2e / heavy-browser** test must go green at least twice in CI before merging — one green run doesn't rule out a flake. This applies only to that class (the real-Chrome `test/fullBrowserHeavyTests/` suites); the deterministic offline/unit/integration tests don't touch a live browser or network, so one green run is enough for them.
24	- A test that can only run remotely (e.g. CI-only) must diagnose itself: on failure, dump the observed state, not just an assertion. It must also be *hang-proof* — bound every `await` (a timeout race) and set a test-level timeout — so a failure fails fast with that diagnostic instead of burning the whole job's timeout. An unbounded await on something that never settles (e.g. a callback that silently never fires) turns a 5-second failure into a 20-minute hang, and each CI-only iteration already costs a full round-trip.
25	- Run a suite you know is slow as **its own command with an explicit timeout well above its measured runtime**, and do the dependency install as a *separate, earlier* call. An agent shell caps a command at a default (order of a couple of minutes) and pushes it to the background when it expires; the reflex is then to start the suite over, so one green result costs double the wall clock with two suites racing each other. Chaining setup in front of the suite is what usually pushes the pair past the cap. If a run does get backgrounded, wait on the one already running rather than launching a second.
26	- To test code that drives a real browser or other external runtime in CI, prefer a *self-authored hermetic input* (e.g. a `data:` URL whose own script reproduces the behavior) over hitting a live third-party target — the live target is non-deterministic and often bot-blocked from a CI/datacenter IP, so it flakes or can't run, while a self-authored input exercises the same engine deterministically. (The SPA-render fallback's CI test renders a `data:` URL whose script fills an empty root, not a real SPA — #310.)
27	- Gate a fuzzy quality metric (a coverage %, not a binary pass) behind a high-watermark: refresh the artifact and ratchet the watermark up locally, keep CI read-only (assert against the committed baseline, never rewrite it), and re-baseline by hand only when a deliberate change legitimately moves it — a number that can only climb catches a silent regression without flapping on noise. When the population it covers can *grow* (e.g. new test cases), store the set the watermark was computed over and gate only over the cases shared with it, so a newly added item is excluded rather than dragging the aggregate below the bar; re-anchor the watermark when the set changes. (A single aggregate watermark can then be re-anchored over a regression bundled into the *same* change as a set change — store per-item bars if that must be caught.)
28	- For behavior a person must sign off on (a third-party integration, an extraction result), keep a layer of declarative, human-reviewed expectation files — distinct from the unit tests, which nobody reads for *intent* — and cover every behavior change with a minimal, representative case there (one behavior per case, no incidental complexity), since that case is what gets reviewed.
29	- When a snapshot/golden test fails because the output *legitimately* moved (the pixels or bytes changed for a real reason), don't quietly regenerate the baseline to go green — an unreviewed baseline change is an unreviewed behavior change. Surface the diff (committed **expected**, newly-rendered **actual**, highlighted **diff**) and get owner approval before re-baselining; until then keep the *reverted* baseline committed so the branch honestly shows the test red-pending — never commit the new baseline first.
30	- When a test asserts exact values extracted from a captured artifact (a cached page, a recorded response), record and commit the artifact *first*, then read the expected values off the committed file — don't hand-write the expectations from memory or a live view and hope they match. Guessing the value desyncs the test from the real fixture; reading it off the committed bytes can't.
31	- A test that maintains a committed artifact should regenerate it into the working tree deterministically (no timestamps, so an unchanged run yields no diff) and skip the write under CI — never shell out to git from a test. Commit the artifact through the normal review flow, like a snapshot.
32	- Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. A surface that is inline-styled SVG, or flexbox-only markup authored for it, renders **bit-exact** through a headless rasterizer (e.g. satori → SVG, resvg → PNG) driven by the shipped code, using **bundled** fonts, never system fonts, and a pinned locale — demand a **zero-pixel** diff there. But that rasterizer has no CSS engine and draws no native widgets: a full shipped page using CSS **grid**, custom properties (`var()`), `@media`, **emoji**, or **form controls** (a range slider, radio, `<select>`) is beyond it — screenshot that with a **headless browser** instead, and allow a *small* diff tolerance (browser antialiasing varies across machines, so it isn't bit-exact). Match the engine to the surface; never reshape the product to fit the rasterizer. (A rasterized popup golden works only because the popup was authored flexbox-only — the moment a surface needs grid/vars/widgets, it needs a browser.) Since the browser goldens aren't gate-able bit-exact and a runner may lack the browser, let those cases **self-skip** where it's absent so the deterministic cases still gate.
33	- To image-golden a surface your code **injects into a host page** (a control mounted into a third-party toolbar), render it against a **committed capture of the real host DOM with its computed styles flattened inline** — the deterministic rasterizer reads only inline styles, and the host's own stylesheet is not yours to ship. Mount it with the **shipped injector** (so the golden proves the placement, not a hand-placed copy), and name the model's boundary honestly: substituted icon-font glyphs, an approximated host chrome (a captured sample is spec, not folklore — the origin lesson of a supported-targets matrix).
34

1	# Chrome extensions
2	
3	Portable, project-agnostic practices for building Chrome (and Chromium) extensions — manifest
4	versions, background/service workers, content scripts, permissions, packaging and store review —
5	true for any extension read cold.
6	
7	> **Releasing, versioning, and Chrome Web Store publication are standardized** — before building
8	> or changing any release/publish machinery in an extension repo, read the
9	> [chrome-store-releases standard](skills/chrome-store-releases/SKILL.md) and copy its canonical
10	> workflows instead of re-deriving them.
11	
12	## Service worker
13	
14	- **Handing a path to a Chrome API or `fetch` from an MV3 service worker** (`importScripts`,
15	  `action.setIcon`) — make it extension-root absolute: a leading slash, or
16	  `chrome.runtime.getURL(...)`. A worker's relative paths resolve against the worker's **own** file
17	  location, not the extension root, and a bare relative path fails silently — it can abort the
18	  worker on import, or make an API call reject while the worker keeps running.
19	
20	- **Wanting `import`/`export` in extension code** — MV3 loads ES modules natively; don't add a
21	  bundler just to use them. Declare the service worker `"type": "module"` and load page/side-panel
22	  scripts with `<script type="module">`; relative imports resolve within the packaged extension.
23	  Content scripts are the exception — they are classic scripts, below.
24	
25	## Content scripts
26	
27	- **Assembling a shared global from several injected content-script files** — **augment** it,
28	  never replace it: merge onto it (e.g. `Object.assign`), not `globalThis.X = {...}`. The files are
29	  re-injected into the page on every activation (e.g. every popup open), so replacing makes each
30	  newly-injected file wipe what earlier files already attached.
31	
32	- **Accumulating state in a file that is re-injected** (e.g. a list a source pushes into) — reset
33	  it at load time.
34	
35	- **Loading ES module code into a content script** — register a tiny **classic loader** whose only
36	  statement is a *dynamic* `import(chrome.runtime.getURL('…'))`. A **registered or static content
37	  script runs as a *classic* script — it can't be an ES module**:
38	  `chrome.scripting.registerContentScripts` and static `content_scripts` inject their files as
39	  classic scripts (there is no `type: 'module'` mode, unlike a page's `<script type="module">` or
40	  the module service worker), so a top-level `import` in one throws
41	  `Uncaught SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module` — **in the host page's
42	  console, not the extension's**. Dynamic `import()` is legal in a classic script, and the module it
43	  pulls in runs in the same content-script isolated world with the content-script `chrome.*` surface
44	  intact.
45	
46	- **Adding an import to a content-script module** — list that module **and its whole transitive
47	  import graph** under `web_accessible_resources` (gated to the target origins), or the fetch is
48	  blocked.
49	
50	- **Keeping that `web_accessible_resources` list correct** — have a test walk the import graph
51	  from the entry module, so a newly-added import can't silently fall out of the list.
52	
53	## Permissions and host access
54	
55	- **Matching a host with `chrome.events.UrlFilter`** — its host operators are **raw string
56	  matches, not domain-boundary matches**: `hostSuffix: "example.com"` also matches
57	  `evilexample.com`, and `declarativeContent`'s `PageStateMatcher.pageUrl` gates an action icon or
58	  page condition on exactly these filters. To mean *apex-or-any-subdomain*, combine
59	  `hostEquals: "example.com"` with `hostSuffix: ".example.com"` (the leading dot forces a label
60	  boundary); never gate a security- or origin-sensitive behavior on a bare `hostSuffix`.
61	
62	- **Running a content script on arbitrary third-party pages without an install-time host warning**
63	  — request access at runtime: declare the origins under `optional_host_permissions` plus the
64	  (silent) `scripting` permission, call `chrome.permissions.request()` **synchronously inside a real
65	  foreground user gesture** (Chrome rejects the request from a service-worker message handler), then
66	  register the script dynamically with `chrome.scripting.registerContentScripts()` — never a
67	  static `content_scripts` entry.
68	
69	- **Starting the service worker when a runtime-granted permission is in play** — reconcile your
70	  stored enabled-flag against the permission actually granted and re-register (or clean up) to
71	  match, on every start. The grant can be revoked from `chrome://extensions` out from under you.
72	
73	- **A fetch to a host you listed failing in-browser** — `host_permissions` does not bypass CORS.
74	  Listing a host lets the extension's fetches *reach* it, but the server must still return CORS
75	  headers for the extension origin (`chrome-extension://<id>`) or the request fails.
76	
77	- **Reaching your *own* backend** — don't add a `host_permissions` entry merely for that: if it
78	  already returns permissive CORS the fetch succeeds without one, and the entry only adds a scary
79	  install-time host-access warning.
80	
81	## Sign-in and tokens
82	
83	- **Authenticating an extension to a JWT-validating backend** (an API Gateway JWT authorizer, any
84	  OIDC-validating server) — obtain a Google **ID token** with `chrome.identity.launchWebAuthFlow`
85	  (`response_type=id_token`) against a Google Cloud OAuth client of type **Web application**,
86	  redirect to `https://<extension-id>.chromiumapp.org/` (from `chrome.identity.getRedirectURL()`),
87	  scope `openid email profile`, and **verify the returned `nonce`**. Pin the extension id with a
88	  manifest `key` so the redirect URI stays fixed. Do **not** use `chrome.identity.getAuthToken` —
89	  it returns an opaque OAuth *access* token (no verifiable signature/`iss`/`aud`) that a JWT
90	  authorizer rejects.
91	
92	- **Refreshing a token silently** (`launchWebAuthFlow({interactive:false})`) — request
93	  `prompt=none`. `prompt=consent` always needs interaction and therefore always fails silently —
94	  reserve it (or omit `prompt`) for the interactive fallback.
95	
96	- **Refreshing silently with more than one account signed in** — pass the remembered account's
97	  email as `login_hint`; otherwise the provider can't tell which session to reuse and forces an
98	  interactive account-picker. Persist the non-secret email from the first successful sign-in.
99	
100	- **Storing a token** — extension storage is unencrypted, so treat tokens as secrets at rest: keep
101	  the bearer/ID token in in-memory `chrome.storage.session` (cleared on browser exit) and persist
102	  only non-secret identifiers (e.g. the account email) to `chrome.storage.local`.
103	
104	- **Wanting a token to survive a browser restart** — re-run the silent flow; don't switch to a
105	  refresh-token flow just for that, which puts a longer-lived credential on disk.
106	
107	## Extension UI surfaces
108	
109	- **Knowing whether your side panel is open** — have the panel open a `Port` on load and read its
110	  connect/disconnect as open/closed. MV3 gives the side panel no is-open/close API, and an action
111	  popup suppresses `action.onClicked`.
112	
113	- **Opening the side panel programmatically** — `chrome.sidePanel.open()` needs Chrome 116+, so
114	  raise `minimum_chrome_version` accordingly.
115	
116	- **Putting a menu on the toolbar icon itself** — create it with
117	  `chrome.contextMenus.create({ contexts: ['action'], … })`; the `contextMenus` permission carries
118	  **no** install-time warning (unlike a broad host permission).
119	
120	- **Recreating those menu items on install or startup** — call `contextMenus.removeAll()` first,
121	  so they self-heal instead of throwing on duplicate ids when the service worker re-runs its top
122	  level.
123	
124	## Introspecting a service worker over CDP
125	
126	- **Awaiting a `chrome.*` callback API inside `Runtime.evaluate`** — don't: they don't reliably
127	  settle when awaited with `awaitPromise: true` (a hang with no internal timeout). Build the awaited
128	  signal from plain promises (`fetch`/`OffscreenCanvas`) instead.
129	
130	- **Reading a worker value from an injected evaluate** — a bare top-level `function`/`const` isn't
131	  reachable from one, so expose what the probe reads as an explicit `globalThis.x = …`.
132	
133	- **Attaching to a dormant worker** — poll for the global rather than reading it once immediately
134	  after attaching. A dormant worker has no globals until it re-runs its top level, and attaching to
135	  it is what starts that.
