2	name: chrome-store-releases
3	description: The Chrome Web Store release standard every extension repo of ours ships — the vendored release workflows and composite actions, .github/release.config, versioning and the packaged artifact, the store secrets, the README install sections, and the manual Chrome Web Store steps. Use when setting up an extension repo to publish, changing or debugging its release pipeline, when asked to "bump version" on an extension repo, or when a cer/ check fires.
4	---
5	
6	# Releasing a Chrome extension to the Web Store
7	
8	Every Chrome-extension repo of ours ships the **same** release pipeline: same workflows, same
9	Chrome Web Store API usage, same secrets, same versioning and artifact rules, same README install
10	sections. This skill is that contract, the setup steps for a new extension repo, and the manual
11	Chrome Web Store actions the automation can't do. The workflow **logic** is authored once, in this
12	pack's [`stubs/`](../../stubs/) — the [orchestrator](../../stubs/workflows/chrome-extension-release.yml), the
13	five `workflow_call`-only **reusable workflows**, and the
14	[report-failure](../../stubs/actions/report-failure/action.yml),
15	[read-release-config](../../stubs/actions/read-release-config/action.yml) and
16	[bump-extension-patch](../../stubs/actions/bump-extension-patch/action.yml) composite actions — and
17	**vendored into each extension repo's own `.github/`**, where the whole pipeline runs with no
18	cross-repo dependency. GitHub only resolves a reusable workflow or composite action from a repo's
19	own `.github/`, so "the logic lives in the pack" means the pack holds the templates and each repo
20	hosts a *managed* copy: the pack keeps every copy in sync — baselining re-materializes on drift via
21	the `chrome-release-vendoring` migration — so a repo **hosts** the pipeline without **owning** it.
22	Treat the vendored `.github/workflows/` + `.github/actions/` set as generated: edit the pack, not
23	the copy. A repo adds only its **required** `.github/release.config` (five explicit keys, **no
24	defaults**). A merged canon change reaches every extension repo through the nightly baselining, not
25	a live `@main` reference. Everything a repo used to carry as workflow values — the version files, the
26	zip location, the test gate, the shipping set, and the previously per-repo `bump`/`filter` scripts
27	— is either pack logic (the bump, and `npm run build`) or an explicit `release.config` key, so no
28	repo ships a bump or filter script any more. Reference implementation:
29	`missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator`; also adopted by `TLDR` and `CrosswordChat`.
30	
31	Naming in the flat `.github/workflows/` namespace: Chrome-specific logic carries the
32	`chrome-extension-` prefix (future publish standards — other stores — will live beside it);
33	genuinely platform-agnostic pieces (`deploy-privacy-page.yml`, the `report-failure` action) keep
34	general names so other standards reuse them as-is. When in doubt, prefix.
35	
36	## The contract
37	
38	**Versioning**
39	
40	- The extension manifest's `version` (`X.Y.Z`) is the single source of truth. The extension's
41	  `package.json` `version` must equal it, enforced by a CI-run guard (a unit test or an inline
42	  workflow check — the repo picks the mechanism, the invariant is fixed).
43	- **The bump belongs to the change, not to the pipeline.** A change that touches a shipped file
44	  (anything under the repo's `ship_paths`) raises the **patch** in the same PR, across the manifest
45	  and `package.json` together. `cer/version-bumped` is what holds that line, and
46	  `node .github/actions/bump-extension-patch/bump.mjs <manifest_path> <package_json_path>` is what
47	  writes it. Merging that PR *is* cutting the release. A change that ships nothing — a README, a
48	  test, a workflow — needs no bump and cuts no release.
49	- **Minor and major are deliberate, and belong to no single change**, so they are the one bump the
50	  pipeline still performs: dispatch **Release to Chrome Store** with `mode: bump` and `part:
51	  minor|major`, which raises the version, pushes it to `main` and packages the result. **"bump
52	  version"** means that dispatch, or the same edit by hand on a branch.
53	- **No workflow writes a version on its own.** The daily run and "Release: Create Package" alike
54	  ship whatever version is on `main`, and no-op when it has already been released. So a shipped
55	  change that forgot its bump is never released — which is the failure `cer/version-bumped` exists
56	  to catch on the PR instead.
57	
58	**Artifact**
59	
60	- `npm run build` produces the zip at the **forced-uniform** standard location
61	  `dist/<kebab-cased repo name>.zip` (e.g. `dist/google-calendar-event-creator.zip`, `dist/tldr.zip`,
62	  `dist/crossword-chat.zip`) — the place/name is derived, not a config choice; a repo's build must
63	  write there. Stable, never version-stamped, so
64	  `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/latest/download/<zip>` is a permanent
65	  newest-build URL. `manifest.json` sits at the zip's top level.
66	- The zip's contents come from a single shipping-set source of truth in `dev/build/release/`,
67	  drift-guarded by a test — nothing dev/test-only ships, and a renamed runtime file fails the
68	  build rather than silently dropping out of the package.
69	- A release is GitHub Release **`vX.Y.Z`**, tagged at the released commit, with auto-generated notes
70	  and **two** assets built from the one tested tree, differing only in the injected `API_BASE_URL`:
71	  the headline **`<zip>`** (the permanent `…/releases/latest/download/<zip>` URL) is built with
72	  `API_BASE_URL` **cleared**, so it keeps the committed **dev** default — the downloadable build is
73	  dev, never prod; **`<zip>-prod.zip`** carries the injected prod `API_BASE_URL` and is the store's
74	  source of truth (the publish job downloads it). So **only the store submission is prod-pointed**;
75	  the signing key + client id are injected into both. (A repo with no `API_BASE_URL` — no backend —
76	  produces two byte-identical zips; the split is a no-op there.)
77	
78	**Workflow** — **one** orchestrator per repo, [`chrome-extension-release.yml`](../../stubs/workflows/chrome-extension-release.yml), named exactly
79	`Release to Chrome Store`. It owns only the triggers; its three `if:`-guarded jobs each call a **local**
80	reusable workflow (`./.github/workflows/…`, all vendored alongside it). The failure reporter keys
81	tracking issues on the **per-operation** names baked into the reusable workflows (`Release: Create
82	Package`, `Release: Publish to Chrome Web Store`, `Release: Daily Auto-Release`) — not on the
83	orchestrator's `name:` — so collapsing to one entry point loses no per-operation triage:
84	
85	| job (trigger) | reusable workflow it calls — what it does |
86	|---|---|
87	| `create-package` (push to `main`; dispatch `mode: package`) | `chrome-extension-create-package.yml` — version guard (a clean no-op unless the manifest version was bumped, so ordinary pushes don't cut a release) → full test gate → build the dev headline `<zip>` + the prod `<zip>-prod.zip` → GitHub Release |
88	| `publish` (dispatch `mode: publish` — the default — with `tag`, `auto_publish`) | `chrome-extension-publish-store.yml` — download the prod `<zip>-prod.zip` (falls back to `<zip>` for pre-split releases) → upload via the store API (publish to users unless `auto_publish: false` → dashboard draft) → refresh the `/privacy/` page (via the `deploy-privacy-page.yml` reusable) |
89	| `daily` (schedule `30 0 * * *`; dispatch `mode: daily`) | `chrome-extension-daily-release.yml` — has the version on `main` been released yet? → if not, calls the two reusable workflows above on `main`'s tip |
90	| `bump` (dispatch `mode: bump` with `part: minor\|major`) | `chrome-extension-bump-version.yml` — raise the minor or major across the manifest + `package.json`, push it to `main`, then `create-package` on that commit |
91	
92	The `create-package` job triggers on **every** push to `main` (no per-repo manifest path in the
93	trigger) and relies on the version guard to no-op unless a bump landed. The privacy page has **no
94	job of its own** and no dedicated option: it redeploys as part of **every** publish, from the same
95	`PRIVACY.md` the listing points at. The publish workflow runs that deploy leg even when the store
96	upload fails (so the `/privacy/` URL goes live before the first publication too — see below). The
97	platform-agnostic `deploy-privacy-page.yml` reusable workflow is vendored alongside the others and
98	called by the publish reusable — a repo never dispatches it directly.
99	
100	- Repo-specific values do **not** travel as `with:` inputs — the reusable workflows read them from
101	  the repo itself via the `read-release-config` action, so the orchestrator is copy-verbatim. They live in a
102	  **required, fully explicit** `.github/release.config` (dotenv) — **five keys, no defaults**, because
103	  a default that "happens to match" a repo's layout silently ships the wrong thing when the layout or
104	  the default later changes:
105	  `manifest_path`, `package_json_path`, `setup_command` (`""` = no install, stated),
106	  `test_command`, `ship_paths`. Two things are **not** keys because they are **forced-uniform
107	  structure**, not a per-repo choice: the **build** is always `npm run build`, and the **zip** lives
108	  at `dist/<kebab repo name>.zip` (both `zip_path` and the asset name are derived).
109	  `cer/release-config` fails the review on a missing file, a missing required key, or an unknown
110	  (typo'd) key.
111	- The one value that stays in the **orchestrator** (not the config file) is `build_env` — KEY=VALUE lines a
112	  repo whose build bakes in release config passes on the `create-package` and `daily` jobs, because
113	  it must reference `${{ vars.* }}` statically. Every listed key must be non-empty or the run fails,
114	  so a repo can't ship a placeholder-configured zip. These are the genuine per-**environment**
115	  values that must not be committed; they live in repository **variables** (Settings → Secrets and
116	  variables → Actions → Variables). Store secrets travel via `secrets: inherit`.
117	- Every unattended workflow (all of the above; not PR CI) reports failures through the
118	  `report-failure` composite action baked into the reusable workflows — a red run must reach a
119	  human, never sit unseen in the Actions list. Each failure opens a **fresh** `workflow-failure`
120	  issue, and any earlier open failure issues for the **same** workflow are closed as duplicates of
121	  it, so the newest failure is always the single open bug to triage. Repos no longer carry a
122	  `report-failure.yml`; a repo's own non-standard unattended workflows use the vendored action
123	  directly (`uses: ./.github/actions/report-failure`).
124	- Daily auto-release semantics: it asks the **release list**, not a file diff — has the version
125	  currently on `main` been released? That is self-healing by construction (a failed day retries the
126	  next with nothing to undo, and a day whose merges shipped nothing carries the version that is
127	  already out and no-ops), and it leaves no window in which the pipeline and the repo disagree about
128	  what the current version is. Release + publish are invoked via `workflow_call` because a
129	  `GITHUB_TOKEN` push triggers no workflows.
130	- `ship_paths` is what `cer/version-bumped` reads to decide whether a change owed a bump, so the
131	  declaration that used to be the daily filter is now the check's scope — one statement of what
132	  ships, read on the PR instead of a day later. A repo whose shipping set is a curated subset (not a
133	  whole directory) lists it there and keeps its build's own ship-set test honest against that list.
134	- The bump is **pack logic**, not a per-repo script: the `bump-extension-patch` composite action
135	  (token-replaces the version in `manifest_path` + `package_json_path`; `part` selects patch, minor
136	  or major, and `--print` reads the current one). It, and the `read-release-config` action, are
137	  dependency-free and run on a bare runner (no `npm ci`). The directory keeps its older
138	  `bump-extension-patch` name because it is vendored into every extension repo, where a rename would
139	  strand the old copy.
140	- Until the four store secrets exist, the publish leg fails **loudly** (a fail-early step lists
141	  the missing names, and the tracking issue nags) — that is the designed state for a repo that
142	  hasn't finished its first manual publication; releases and zips still work.
143	
144	**Chrome Web Store API** — uploads go through `chrome-webstore-upload-cli@3`
145	(`npx --yes chrome-webstore-upload-cli@3 upload --source dist/<zip> [--auto-publish]`), which
146	reads env `EXTENSION_ID` / `CLIENT_ID` / `CLIENT_SECRET` / `REFRESH_TOKEN` — set from the four
147	repository **secrets**, same names in every repo:
148	`CHROME_EXTENSION_ID`, `CHROME_CLIENT_ID`, `CHROME_CLIENT_SECRET`, `CHROME_REFRESH_TOKEN`.
149	
150	**Privacy page** — the policy source is `dev/build/release/store_artifacts/PRIVACY.md`; a Jekyll
151	`permalink: /privacy/` pins the public URL `https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/privacy/`
152	independent of the file's location. The store listing's Privacy-tab URL points **there**, never
153	at a `blob/main` link. The page redeploys on every store publish — the publish workflow's
154	privacy-deploy leg runs regardless of whether the upload leg succeeds, so it also brings the URL up
155	for the very first publication.
156	One-time: repo Settings → Pages → Source = "GitHub Actions".
157	
158	**Store listing & permission justifications live in the dashboard, not the repo** — the listing
159	copy (name, summary, detailed description, category), the graphic-asset choices, and the
160	Privacy-practices answers (single-purpose statement, a justification for **every** permission the
161	manifest requests — `permissions`, `host_permissions`, and `optional_*` alike — the remote-code
162	answer, data-usage declarations, reviewer notes) are all Chrome Web Store dashboard state. We keep
163	**no** repo copy of them: a mirror only drifts from the dashboard it duplicates. They are authored
164	once, at the first publication (tracked by a one-time issue — see setup below), and edited in the
165	dashboard thereafter. What the repo *does* hold and enforce is the privacy policy and its
166	agreement with the manifest:
167	
168	- `dev/build/release/store_artifacts/PRIVACY.md` is the privacy policy, deployed verbatim as the
169	  public `/privacy/` page the listing points at.
170	
171	**Store assets & icons** — required inventory: a 128 px store icon; the manifest icons the
172	extension ships (16/32/48/128), living inside the extension source where the manifest points;
173	at least one 1280×800 (or 640×400) screenshot; optionally 440×280 small and 1400×560 marquee
174	promo tiles. Listing-only images live in `store_artifacts/`; shipped icons live in the extension
175	source. Every asset comes from a **committed, deterministic generator script** — regenerate and
176	commit, never hand-edit a generated PNG. The generator's tech is the repo's choice (the
177	reference repo draws with stdlib-only Python; CrosswordChat rasterizes SVG/HTML with headless
178	Chromium); what's fixed is that every asset is reproducible from the repo.
179	
180	**Layout** — release machinery lives in `dev/build/release/`: the zip builder + shipping-set
181	module (with its test), and `store_artifacts/` (`PRIVACY.md`, listing screenshots, icon/asset
182	generators). No per-repo bumper or shipped-paths filter: the bump is vendored pack logic, and
183	`ship_paths` in `.github/release.config` is the one statement of what ships. No per-repo release doc: the concrete names and paths live in
184	`manifest.json`/`package.json` and the required `.github/release.config`, and the shared procedure
185	lives once, in this guide — a repo copy would only drift from it.
186	
187	## README template
188	
189	Every extension repo's README carries these two sections, same wording, repo values filled in:
190	
191	```markdown
192	## Install
193	
194	**[Install from the Chrome Web Store →](<store listing URL>)**
195	
196	Or load the latest development build:
197	
198	1. Download [the latest release zip](https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/latest/download/<zip>)
199	   and extract it — it unpacks to a folder with `manifest.json` at its top.
200	2. Open `chrome://extensions`, enable **Developer mode** (top right), click
201	   **Load unpacked**, and select that folder.
202	
203	## Releasing
204	
205	The version users see is [`<manifest path>`](<manifest path>)'s `version`. A change that touches a
206	shipped file raises it in the same PR; merging that PR cuts GitHub Release `vX.Y.Z` with `<zip>`
207	attached, and the daily auto-release ships that version to the Chrome Web Store on its own.
208	```
209	
210	Until the extension's first store publication, replace the store line with:
211	
212	```markdown
213	*Not yet on the Chrome Web Store — the listing goes live after the first manual publish (tracked
214	in the repo's first-publication issue).*
215	```
216	
217	## Setting up a new extension repo
218	
219	1. Declare the pack in `.claudinite-settings.json`; baselining then **vendors the release set** — the
220	   [orchestrator](../../stubs/workflows/chrome-extension-release.yml) plus the reusable workflows under
221	   [`stubs/workflows/`](../../stubs/workflows/) and the composite actions under
222	   [`stubs/actions/`](../../stubs/actions/) — into this repo's own `.github/`. (Setting up before the next
223	   nightly pass? Copy those two trees yourself; there are no tokens to replace.) Then write the
224	   **required** `.github/release.config` (dotenv) with **all five** keys, explicitly — no defaults:
225	   `manifest_path`, `package_json_path`, `setup_command` (`""` = no install), `test_command`,
226	   `ship_paths`. (The build is always `npm run build`, and the zip lives at the derived
227	   `dist/<kebab repo name>.zip`, so neither is a key.) If the build bakes in per-environment config,
228	   uncomment the `build_env` block on the `create-package` and `daily` jobs of the orchestrator (the
229	   only vendored file a repo edits) and set the matching repository **variables** (see step 5).
230	2. Create `dev/build/release/` — zip builder + shipping-set module (with its test) and
231	   `store_artifacts/` with `PRIVACY.md` and the icon/asset generators — adapting from the reference
232	   repo's `dev/build/release/`. **No** per-repo bumper or shipped-paths filter (the bump is
233	   vendored pack logic); a curated shipping set is expressed as `ship_paths` in `release.config`, kept honest
234	   against the build by the repo's own ship-set test. No `releasing.md` and no `STORE-LISTING.md`:
235	   the release procedure lives in this guide, and the listing copy / permission justifications are
236	   dashboard state (above).
237	3. Wire `npm run build` to produce the zip at the standard `dist/<kebab repo name>.zip` (a monorepo
238	   sets a root `build` that delegates, e.g. `npm --prefix client run build`) and set `test_command`
239	   to the repo's full release gate. Add the two README sections above.
240	4. One-time GitHub setup: Pages → Source = "GitHub Actions". The four `CHROME_*` secrets come
241	   later, after the first manual publish. (No cross-repo Actions access to configure — the whole
242	   pipeline is vendored, so it never calls another repo's reusable workflows.)
243	5. Open the **first-publication tracking issue** (idempotent — search the tracker first, skip if
244	   one already exists, open or closed) so the one-time manual setup below is tracked as state, not
245	   carried as a repo file. Its checklist:
246	   - Set the four `CHROME_*` **secrets** (minted below) — Settings → Secrets and variables →
247	     Actions → Secrets.
248	   - **Only if the orchestrator uses `build_env`**: set the repository **variables** it references. These
249	     are automatable where API access exists — the issue carries a ready-to-run script, e.g.
250	     `gh variable set API_BASE_URL --repo <owner>/<repo> --body "https://…"` (repeat per key) —
251	     rather than a click-through, so the one manual part is minting the store credentials, not
252	     copying config into Settings.
253	   - Do the "First publication" steps below, then close the issue. From then on the daily pipeline
254	     owns routine shipping.
255	
256	> A repo's **own** first-publication runbook — a go-live checklist, an account/credentials setup
257	> guide — is the same do-then-close artifact by another name: first-publication *guidance*, not
258	> standing reference. Once the extension is live it's spent; fold anything durable into the
259	> standing architecture/README docs it already defers to, then remove the file. (That a cleanup
260	> makes you fix references *into* such a doc is the cue to ask whether the doc itself is in scope
261	> for removal — not to polish it.)
262	
263	## Manual actions — publishing to the Chrome Web Store
264	
265	The steps the automation cannot do, distilled from the path actually run for the reference
266	extension; the upstream reference is
267	[Using the Chrome Web Store Publish API](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/webstore/using-api).
268	
269	### First publication (once per extension)
270	
271	1. Register a developer account at the
272	   [developer dashboard](https://chrome.google.com/webstore/devconsole) (one-time $5 fee).
273	2. **Add new item** → upload the release zip. If the extension pins its ID with a manifest
274	   `key` (needed when OAuth redirect URIs depend on a stable ID — see
275	   [the chrome-extension pack RULES](../../RULES.md)), the **first** upload must NOT contain the
276	   `key`: the store assigns the ID at first upload, and you copy the dashboard's Package-tab
277	   public key back into the build afterwards. Record the 32-char item ID → the
278	   `CHROME_EXTENSION_ID` secret.
279	3. Complete the listing — 128px store icon, name, summary, detailed description, category,
280	   ≥ 1280×800 screenshot — authoring the copy **directly in the dashboard** (this is where it
281	   lives; the repo keeps no copy). Screenshots and icons come from `store_artifacts/`.
282	4. Privacy tab: write the single-purpose statement, a justification for **every** permission the
283	   manifest requests, and the data-usage declarations, directly in the dashboard; set the
284	   **Privacy policy** field (bottom of the tab) to the `/privacy/` Pages URL — the same policy
285	   `PRIVACY.md` deploys. **Before submitting**: bring the privacy page up by running the **Release**
286	   workflow once with **mode: publish** — its privacy-deploy leg runs even though the store-upload leg
287	   fails at this stage (no store item or secrets yet — the designed pre-publication state), so the
288	   `/privacy/` page goes live. Load the URL in a browser to confirm it's live, and paste that exact
289	   permalink — never a guessed path. Google re-fetches this URL on **every** publish, and an
290	   unreachable link fails the publish (see [When a store publish fails](#when-a-store-publish-fails)).
291	5. Submit for review — approval takes hours to a few days (`ITEM_PENDING_REVIEW` = success).
292	   While the item is **pending review the API rejects uploads** — hold the pipeline dry run
293	   until the first review completes. Every subsequent upload must carry a **strictly higher**
294	   version, which is why every shipped change raises one (`cer/version-bumped`); a "version must be
295	   greater" rejection on a dry run is a **pass** — it proves the credential wiring works
296	   end to end.
297	
298	### Minting the API credentials (once per extension)
299	
300	Browser-only — no local tooling needed. Two standing rules for every step below:
301	
302	- Every "sign in with Google" must use the **same Google account that owns the store listing**,
303	  and will hit a **"Google hasn't verified this app"** interstitial — click **Advanced** →
304	  **"Go to \<app\> (unsafe)"** → **Allow**. That's fine and permanent: you are this OAuth app's
305	  only user, so **ignore every verification prompt and never start verification** — an
306	  unverified app's tokens work indefinitely.
307	- Before acting on any Cloud-console page, confirm the **top-bar project picker** shows the
308	  project created in step 1.
309	
310	**Google Cloud setup:**
311	
312	1. **Create a project**: <https://console.cloud.google.com/projectcreate> — any name, keep
313	   "No organization" → **Create**. Confirm the top-bar project picker switched to it.
314	2. **Enable the Chrome Web Store API**:
315	   <https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/library/chromewebstore.googleapis.com> → **Enable**.
316	3. **Configure the OAuth consent screen** (the console now brands this "Google Auth
317	   Platform"): <https://console.cloud.google.com/auth/overview> → **Get started** → app name +
318	   support email → Audience: **External** → contact email → agree → **Create**.
319	4. **Publish the app to production**: <https://console.cloud.google.com/auth/audience> →
320	   **Publish app** → **Confirm**. Left in "Testing", refresh tokens silently expire after
321	   7 days — the unattended daily release dies a week later.
322	5. **Create the OAuth client**: <https://console.cloud.google.com/auth/clients> → **Create
323	   client** → type **Web application** (NOT Desktop — Desktop clients can't take custom
324	   redirect URIs; the client type makes no difference to `chrome-webstore-upload-cli`, the
325	   refresh-token grant is identical) → add authorized redirect URI exactly
326	   `https://developers.google.com/oauthplayground` → **Create**. The client ID and secret are
327	   `CHROME_CLIENT_ID` / `CHROME_CLIENT_SECRET`.
328	
329	**Mint the refresh token in the OAuth 2.0 Playground:**
330	
331	1. Open <https://developers.google.com/oauthplayground> → gear icon (top right) → check
332	   **Use your own OAuth credentials** → paste the client ID + secret.
333	2. In Step 1, ignore the API list: type `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/chromewebstore` into
334	   **Input your own scopes** → **Authorize APIs** → sign in as the listing owner → past the
335	   unverified interstitial → **Allow**.
336	3. Step 2 → **Exchange authorization code for tokens** → copy the **Refresh token** (starts
337	   `1//`). Ignore the access token — it expires hourly; the CLI mints its own.
338	4. **Empty Refresh-token field?** Consent wasn't force-prompted: in the gear panel set
339	   **Force prompt: Consent** and redo the authorize step.
340	
341	Add all four values as repository secrets at
342	`https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/settings/secrets/actions/new`:
343	`CHROME_EXTENSION_ID`, `CHROME_CLIENT_ID`, `CHROME_CLIENT_SECRET`, `CHROME_REFRESH_TOKEN`.
344	
345	**Alternative — local Node**: `npx chrome-webstore-upload-keys` walks the same flow from a
346	terminal (it needs the client to be a **Desktop app**, whose `http://localhost` redirect it
347	uses). Use it only when a Node-equipped machine is at hand; the Playground route above is the
348	default because it assumes nothing about the operator's machine.
349	
350	### Routine shipping
351	
352	- Nothing to do for accumulated work: each shipped change landed with its own patch bump, so the
353	  daily auto-release ships whatever version is on `main` the moment it is not yet released.
354	- A deliberate release now: merge the shipped change (which carries its bump, and cutting the
355	  GitHub Release is what merging it does) → run **Release to Chrome Store** with **mode: publish**
356	  from its dispatch page,
357	  `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/actions/workflows/chrome-extension-release.yml` (blank tag = latest release).
358	- A new feature set or a new generation: **"bump version"** — the same workflow with **mode: bump**
359	  and `part: minor|major`, which raises it, pushes it and packages the result.
360	- Once the store approves, Chrome auto-pushes the update to installed users within hours — no
361	  reinstall.
362	
363	### When a store publish fails
364	
365	- **HTTP 400 `Publish condition not met: Privacy policy link is not reachable.`** — Google
366	  fetches the listing's privacy-policy URL at publish time, and re-checks it on **every**
367	  publish. Fix it on the item's **Privacy** tab in the
368	  [developer dashboard](https://chrome.google.com/webstore/devconsole)
369	  (`https://chrome.google.com/webstore/devconsole/<publisher-id>/<item-id>/edit/privacy`,
370	  bottom field, "Privacy policy"): set it to the exact live `/privacy/` permalink → **Save
371	  draft** → re-run the publish.
372	- **Upload rejected while `ITEM_PENDING_REVIEW`** — the API can't upload while a review is in
373	  flight; wait for the review to complete, then re-run.
374	- **"version must be greater" than the live one** — expected whenever the zip's version isn't
375	  strictly higher; on a credentials dry run this is success. Otherwise the version on `main` is one
376	  the store already has: the change that needed shipping never raised it, so raise it in a PR (or
377	  dispatch `mode: bump`) rather than re-running the publish.
378	
379	### When a change touches the extension's permissions
380	
381	Any PR that changes the manifest's `permissions`, `host_permissions`, or `optional_*`:
382	
383	1. Adding a permission trips `cer/permission-added-store-issue` (advisory): open a tracking issue
384	   for the manual dashboard step — the Privacy-practices tab must carry a written justification
385	   for the new permission, and the store blocks publishing the new version until it does, so the
386	   next store publish (daily or manual) stalls on it. (If the daily pipeline hits it first, the
387	   failed publish lands on its `workflow-failure` tracking issue; the proactive issue beats the
388	   reactive one.) After updating the dashboard, re-run the publish.
389	2. Expect deeper store review than a plain code update — permission changes re-open scrutiny.
390	3. A new **required** permission that carries an install-time warning disables the extension
391	   for existing users until each one re-approves it — prefer `optional_permissions` /
392	   `optional_host_permissions` requested at runtime (`chrome.permissions.request`) when the
393	   feature allows.
394

1	# claude-code-web-users-support — for the people working on this from the web
2	
3	A Claude Code **web** session runs for a signed-in person, in a managed container. A
4	terminal session does neither. This pack is where the capabilities that depend on that
5	difference live — anything a project can offer only when the session knows **who** is
6	here, or only because the environment it runs in is one somebody configured.
7	
8	## Personal interaction preferences
9	
10	This project reads each person's **personal interaction preferences** at session start:
11	how they want to be worked with — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, the
12	phrases they use to trigger a defined command. If the current user has a file in the
13	store, its contents are already in this session's context, injected under this pack's
14	marker by [`session-start.mjs`](session-start.mjs).
15	
16	**They are not project conventions.** Conventions belong to the packs that own each
17	subject and load as prose. What this carries is *personal*: the same rules travel with
18	a person across every project they work in, and two people on one project can want
19	different things. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project
20	convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the preference owns only the
21	trigger phrase.
22	
23	**The pack holds an address, not the content.** Preferences belong to a group of people
24	rather than to any one repository, so this project's declaration names the **store** —
25	a repo, and a path inside it holding one `<email>.md` per person:
26	
27	```json
28	{ "id": "claude-code-web-users-support", "config": { "repo": "owner/name", "path": "preferences" } }
29	```
30	
31	`path` is optional and defaults to `preferences`. Reading is **local-first**: when this
32	repo *is* the store, the working copy wins over the default branch, so an edit in
33	progress is what the session sees.
34	
35	**Every miss is fail-soft.** No identity (a terminal session has none), no configured
36	store, no file for this person, a fetch that fails — each is one plain-text note and the
37	session proceeds on default interaction behavior. Nothing here is load-bearing, and a
38	nice-to-have must never be able to stop a session from starting.
39	
40	### If this repo *is* the store
41	
42	The file name is the **whole address**: the reader builds `<path>/<email>.md` from the
43	identity the harness supplies, and there is no index, no registry and no fallback. So
44	every file under `path` is either the store's own `README.md` or one person's
45	`<identity>.md`; anything else sits in the tree looking fine and is never opened. Two
46	consequences worth holding: the name must be that person's identity **exactly**, because
47	it becomes a case-sensitive `raw.githubusercontent.com` path segment that a local
48	checkout would happily serve either way; and the store is **flat**, because grouping
49	people into subdirectories makes their files unaddressable.
50	
51	### Adding or changing a preference
52	
53	Edit that person's file **in the store repo** — never here, and never in the canon. One
54	distilled preference per bullet, in the imperative: a preference is a rule the assistant
55	can act on, not a description of a mood. A preference that turns out to be a project
56	convention in disguise belongs in the pack that owns its subject instead.
57	
58	## The web environment's Setup script
59	
60	Only a managed container has a **Setup script** field, and the web base image ships no
61	toolchains — so a web session can run a project's tests only if somebody pasted one in.
62	The body to paste is [`environment-setup-command.sh`](environment-setup-command.sh),
63	whole and unedited: it installs every active pack's declared requirement, so it is
64	identical for every project and never changes as those requirements do. Re-paste it (and
65	rebuild) when a session-start check reports a missing requirement — never hand-edit a
66	project-specific step into it; that step belongs in the owning pack's `env` declaration.
67

1	# claudinite-fleet-sheepdog — the fleet enforcer marker
2	
3	Declaring this pack marks a repo as the **fleet enforcer**: the one repo that covers and maintains
4	every repo under an owner. What the pack *is* — its six sweeps, their schedule, their reports, the
5	config schema — is [README.md](README.md). This file is what a session **here** has to get right.
6	
7	## Configuring the fleet
8	
9	- **Keeping a repo out of the fleet** — add its full `owner/name` to `exclude` on this pack's
10	  config entry. Nothing else opts a repo out: an archived or forked repo is reported as out of scope
11	  but still walked, and a repo that simply never adopted is `uncovered`, which is a finding rather
12	  than a choice. If a repo should not be measured, say so in `exclude` and the reports stop asking
13	  about it.
14	
15	- **Adding or changing a `packSeeds` entry** — get it right *before* the sweep next runs. The
16	  sweep seeds and never overrides, so a wrong seed reaches each member exactly once and then sticks;
17	  correcting it here un-writes nothing, and undoing it is a change in every member's repo. Land the
18	  entry and its own declaration together, then read the next run's report rather than assuming.
19	
20	- **Declaring a pack this fleet also seeds** — write the same config in both places, spelling
21	  every default out on both sides rather than leaving one implicit. `seeds-agree` compares them
22	  literally, because nothing in this pack may know what one pack's absent key means. A pack the
23	  fleet standardizes on but this repo does not itself run has nothing to agree with, and is fine.
24	
25	## Acting on what a sweep reports
26	
27	- **Acting on an `add-packs` work-list issue** — the work is a declaration and a reviewed PR **in
28	  the named member**, never here. A session in this repo is scoped to this repo, so if every item
29	  names another repo there is nothing here to do: say the scope is the blocker rather than writing
30	  to the issues, which are the only thing within reach and are not the work.
31	
32	- **Acting on a scanned pack suggestion** — it is a recommendation, never a verdict.
33	  A fingerprint is a way to *suspect* a pack is wanted; whether to declare it is the member's call,
34	  and closing the issue `not planned` is a standing answer the scan honours rather than re-opening.
35	  A **forced** addition is the other thing entirely — a decision already made — so adopt what
36	  its issue says instead of re-judging whether it was wanted.
37	
38	- **Reading `unknown` in a report** — it means the sweep could not look, not that it looked and
39	  found nothing. Never convert one into a verdict: a repo whose declaration could not be read is
40	  neither covered nor uncovered, an undecided fingerprint is not a non-match, and a member the
41	  pack-seed sweep could not reach is not converged. Fix the access and re-run.
42	
43	- **Judging whether a member is behind** — compare `engineVersion` and `packVersions` against
44	  canon, never the age of its stamped `ref`. The update flows deliberately never rewrite `ref` or
45	  `updated`, so the stamp is provenance — which commit first vendored the mount — and stays
46	  frozen on a member that is perfectly current. Its age measures nothing, and measuring it
47	  calls the whole fleet behind on one arbitrary day.
48	
49	- **Answering why the fleet did not move** — read the member's own artifacts first: its
50	  declaration, its stamp, the runs on its head sha. This repo dispatches; each member converges
51	  itself, with its own token and its own delivery policy. Propose a settings change as a conclusion,
52	  never as the diagnosis.
53	
54	## Running the manual levers
55	
56	- **Pushing canon to the whole fleet now** — create the work item, from a checkout of this repo:
57	
58	  ```
59	  node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/create-work-item.mjs claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/fleet-baseline
60	  ```
61	
62	  Add `--context "REPOS=owner/a owner/b"` to narrow it (space-separated: a Context line splits on
63	  commas), `--context "DRY_RUN=true"` to see the list without dispatching, or
64	  `--context "INCLUDE_DORMANT=true"` to reach members that stopped their own scheduler on purpose.
65	  Both knobs are read from the item's Context and nowhere else — an item created without them runs
66	  unscoped and live. It queues one
67	  run per member and does not wait; each member reports its own outcome in its own repo. A member
68	  with nothing to do converges to a cheap no-op, so over-using it is wasteful rather than unsafe.
69	
70	- **Adding a pack across the fleet** — create a `fleet-add-missing-packs` item with
71	  `--context "ADD_PACKS=…"` rather than editing anything. No pack is named anywhere in this pack's
72	  code: every id comes from config or from the item's own Context, which is what keeps the
73	  enforcer from becoming a second place packs are known.
74	
75	## Credentials
76	
77	- **Granting or repairing `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN`** — a fine-grained PAT spanning the owner's
78	  repositories, granted exactly what [`fleet-token.mjs`](fleet-token.mjs)'s table names — the only
79	  place the permissions are written, because a per-sweep subset is always a defensible answer and
80	  never the right one. Grant it whole: the token is granted once, for the pack.
81	
82	- **A sweep reporting `403` or `no-permission`** — the grant is short a permission, which the
83	  error names. It is a grant to fix once, so widen the token rather than re-running: no sweep
84	  retries, because a work list nobody will act on is not a green outcome.
85

1	---
2	name: extract-from-activity
3	description: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
4	---
5	
6	# Extract lessons from repo activity
7	
8	The **artifact** half of lesson extraction: mine what a window of work left behind — commits, the PRs
9	merged in it, the issue discussion around them — for durable, reusable lessons, and fold each into the
10	repo's **own local packs**. Its sibling [extract-from-conversations](../extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md)
11	mines the *dialogue*; this one never sees a conversation, only what the work committed.
12	
13	The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
14	surface lives are shared with that sibling and stay canonical in
15	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't re-derive it. What follows is only
16	what reading *artifacts* adds.
17	
18	## Capture at the repo's own level
19	
20	Write each lesson at whatever level reads naturally for this repo — refer to its files, services, or
21	mechanics wherever that's what makes the lesson clear. Don't force either extreme: don't contort a lesson
22	to be hyper-specific, and don't polish it into a general, portable rule. Making a lesson portable is the
23	growth lifecycle's **promote** stage, done canon-side later over whatever merged here; here, just capture
24	it usefully and let promotion lift whatever turns out to travel.
25	
26	## Read the window — and read merged PRs properly
27	
28	Work only the window you were handed (a scheduled run gets it as binding scope in the work item's
29	Context; an owner's ask names it in words). Never widen it.
30	
31	1. **The commits** — full bodies, and the diff wherever a fix is non-obvious.
32	2. **The PRs merged in the window** — read these *first* and read them *whole*: the diff **and** the
33	   review discussion. A merged PR is usually the window's richest lesson source, because it records what
34	   was tried, what a reviewer pushed back on, and why the landed shape won. A verdict reached in review
35	   is a lesson already argued; the commit alone shows only the winner.
36	3. **The issue activity** it names — the comments changed on those numbers.
37	
38	## What artifacts signal — and what they don't
39	
40	The signals worth converting here are the ones an artifact can carry: a fix whose diff is small but whose
41	*reason* is not obvious from the code; a review comment that names a convention the author missed; a
42	revert or a follow-up fix that says the first shape was wrong; a PR that grew several rounds because its
43	approach was re-decided mid-flight.
44	
45	**An already-settled, already-enforced implementation choice is not a lesson.** If a check or a test
46	already pins the shape — which roots a CI sweep walks, which contract a construction must satisfy — and
47	all that is left to say is *why it looks like that*, that explanation belongs as a comment at the
48	implementation site, not as prose in a pack. A rule earns its place by steering a **future** decision or
49	catching a **repeatable** mistake, not by narrating a past one that is already locked in.
50	
51	Wall-time and dialogue friction (a clarifying round-trip, a backtrack, a wait sat through) leave no trace
52	in a diff. Don't infer them from artifacts — that is the conversation sibling's territory, working from
53	logs that actually carry the timestamps.
54	
55	## Landing it
56	
57	Route each keeper down the ladder in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — a declared
58	check first, a custom code rule only where patterns can't say it, then pack skill, prose last — into the
59	local pack whose territory owns it. Write more checks and less prose, and keep each addition terse and in
60	the repo's own voice.
61	
62	A new check ships **green or not at all**: see it fail on a violating fixture and pass on a clean one. A
63	rule that cannot be made confident lands as prose instead — never as a broken check.
64	
65	Finding nothing is a perfectly good and common outcome; a duplicate or invented "lesson" is worse than
66	adding nothing.
67
