1	# web-scraping — taking data from a site you don't own
2	
3	The facet: a project whose input is another organisation's website, reached without a
4	contract. There is no support channel, no changelog and no SLA, so every rule below is about
5	**reducing what you have to re-learn** — from the site, from the network, and from your own
6	pipeline — when it changes underneath you.
7	
8	A default to adapt, not a contract. Language-agnostic: "fetch", "parse" and "normalize" mean
9	whatever they mean on your stack.
10	
11	## Finding the data surface
12	
13	- **Adding a source, or deciding what to parse** — scraping rendered markup is the **last**
14	  resort. Prefer, in order: the hydration blob a server-rendered app embeds in the page, then
15	  the JSON/GraphQL endpoint a single-page app fetches its rows from, and only then the markup
16	  — where you prefer the page's self-describing metadata (JSON-LD, `og:` tags) over element
17	  positions, because metadata survives a redesign and `.results > div:nth-child(2)` does not.
18	  Finding that surface on a new site is a one-off reconnaissance job with its own procedure,
19	  the [`map-a-data-source`](skills/map-a-data-source/SKILL.md) skill.
20	
21	- **A rendered-snapshot expectation shifting after a re-record** — rendered output is **not
22	  deterministic**, so treat the shift the way you'd treat a markup change: re-review it, don't
23	  assume a regression.
24	
25	- **Learning something non-obvious by probing the service** — write it down in a reference doc
26	  beside the scripts: endpoints, auth, the field surface, the enum values. Keep it complete
27	  enough that **nothing needs to re-probe the live service to answer a question**. The
28	  expensive part of this work is the knowledge rather than the code, and re-probing is slow,
29	  rate-limited, sometimes blocked, and occasionally the thing that gets you banned.
30	
31	## Fetching
32	
33	- **Writing the fetch itself** — browser-like headers, a randomized delay between requests, and
34	  exponential backoff on retry. Route **all** outbound page/API fetching through a single
35	  module, so swapping the vendor, the proxy or the credential is one edit with one place to
36	  test.
37	
38	- **Deciding whether to retry a failed request** — retry only what can improve. A gateway or
39	  proxy failure (408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504) is worth another attempt; any other 4xx is about
40	  your request and will answer the same way forever.
41	
42	- **Porting a fetch to a language-level HTTP client** — carry the retry policy across the
43	  rewrite. `curl --retry` covers exactly that status set and the port silently drops all of it,
44	  so the first transient 500 the old command would have ridden out kills the run.
45	
46	- **Setting the retry budget** — attempts times per-attempt timeout, plus the waits, must fit
47	  inside whatever hard limit kills the process, and the backoff should be injectable so tests
48	  exercise the retry path without sleeping through it.
49	
50	- **One item in a batch failing to fetch** — record and continue. Log the reason per item and
51	  emit a report; one unfetchable item should not abandon the batch.
52	
53	- **A sandbox refusing the target host** — an agent sandbox is commonly **bot-blocked**, and its
54	  egress proxy may refuse the host outright. That refusal is policy: **do not route around it**,
55	  not with a local fetch and not with an ad-hoc workflow spun up to reach the host. Give the
56	  fetch one sanctioned home — a scheduled job or workflow on a runner, with the credential in
57	  repository secrets — and let sessions read the committed raw records instead.
58	
59	- **A fetch that works on your machine and fails from CI** — a 403/400 or a CAPTCHA wall from a
60	  runner or a sandbox is usually the *datacenter IP* being blocked, not the headers, so tuning
61	  them is wasted work. **Reaching a commercial rendering proxy** is the standard answer: a
62	  residential lane clears the IP block, and these services usually execute JavaScript too, so a
63	  single-page app records real content. Ask it to render, and give it a wait-for-selector when
64	  the content you want arrives late. A target that stays blocked even through the proxy is
65	  un-cacheable: say so and stop, rather than hunting for another route.
66	
67	- **Needing many items from a service with no list endpoint** — no bulk endpoint is not the same
68	  as no bulk request. GraphQL lets one document alias the same field many times, and many REST
69	  APIs accept a multi-id parameter. The cap is usually undocumented, so **halve a rejected batch
70	  and retry** — that keeps batch size a throughput knob and never an accuracy one.
71	
72	- **A fetch that cannot produce a page at all** — a bot wall, a dead URL, an empty render is a
73	  dead end, not a pipeline failure: mark the item for a human and **exit successfully**. Failing
74	  the run converges on the same human signal while also implying the pipeline broke, when in
75	  fact it correctly declined. The rest of the batch should still land.
76	
77	## Reading what came back
78	
79	- **Deciding whether a fetch succeeded** — a 200 is not success. An anti-bot interstitial arrives
80	  as a normal-looking 200 (or a 403/503) whose body is a challenge page, and caching it stores
81	  garbage that looks like data. Match the known markers in the first few KB and report it as a
82	  distinct failure reason.
83	
84	- **Getting an empty body back** — nothing rendered. Treat it as a failure of that fetch rather
85	  than as an empty result, and don't retry it: a successful-but-empty response will keep being
86	  successful and empty.
87	
88	- **Choosing which field to read** — prefer the authoritative status enum over the summarizing
89	  convenience boolean, which is routinely wrong: an item can report "not sold out" while its
90	  status says there is nothing left to sell. Take the enum's legal values from the service's own
91	  options endpoint rather than from what you happened to see.
92	
93	- **Filtering rows by a status** — deny-list the bad statuses, don't allow-list the good ones,
94	  and log the set actually observed. A new status then defaults to usable and shows up in your
95	  logs, instead of silently dropping rows.
96	
97	- **Reading a numeric field** — numbers may arrive as strings. Parse; don't assume the JSON type.
98	
99	- **Reducing a set to its "cheapest" or "first"** — that value can be a special case rather than
100	  a value. Filter to what the field means before you reduce over it: a zero-priced accessibility
101	  companion band makes the cheapest ticket for every show free.
102	
103	## Normalizing what you read
104	
105	- **Converting an instant to the domain's local time** — instants usually arrive in UTC while
106	  your domain thinks in local wall-clock. Do the conversion in one function at the ingestion
107	  boundary and have everything downstream speak local time. Slicing digits out of the string
108	  files everything an hour off during daylight saving, and **the result looks completely
109	  plausible** — nothing throws, nothing is empty, the data is simply wrong. Because the failure
110	  is silent, keep a **known-answer probe**: an item whose correct value you know independently
111	  (something named after its own time, a figure published elsewhere), checked after every fresh
112	  pull. "Exactly once" cuts both ways — a stage downstream of the boundary that parses,
113	  re-offsets or re-reads a stored value as UTC is the same bug from the other end.
114	
115	- **Taking a "now"** — read it in the domain's zone rather than off the device clock. A reviewer
116	  in the same zone as the developer cannot see the difference, which is how a device clock
117	  survives review.
118	
119	- **Parsing a value whose format is ambiguous** — read it by what the page declares, centrally;
120	  never per-source, never guessed. A numeric slash date whose parts are both ≤ 12 (`05/07/2026`)
121	  has no intrinsic answer, so resolve it from a *positive* signal the document gives you (an
122	  explicit region in `<html lang>` or `og:locale`, a non-English language) and keep the default
123	  when the signal is absent or region-less, rather than inferring one from the host or the
124	  venue. Put that resolution in one helper the whole pipeline threads, so a new source cannot
125	  invent its own reading. A trailing `Z` or `+00:00` is *serialization*, not a claim about the
126	  subject's zone: it neither supplies the zone nor vetoes deriving one from what the page says
127	  about the place.
128	
129	- **Changing the conversion** — it is a **full-snapshot change**. Committed derived data is
130	  generator output, so the fix isn't done until the raw record is re-run through the new
131	  conversion and every downstream artifact regenerated. Expect the boundary to move records
132	  between partitions — items at the end of a day land in the next one, and may fall outside the
133	  range your day-partitioned files cover — and check that rather than reading it as data loss.
134	
135	- **Emitting a value your pipeline hasn't reached yet** — missing is its own state: *unknown*,
136	  never folded into *free*, *empty* or *false*. Sources keep adding rows after your last full
137	  pass, so gaps are normal and permanent. Carry unknown through the whole stack — omit the key
138	  rather than emitting a default — and let each consumer render it as its own thing.
139	
140	## What lands on disk, and when it refreshes
141	
142	- **Deciding what a fetch writes to disk** — two forms, separated deliberately. The fetched
143	  artifact (page HTML, raw response pages) is a **cache**: git-ignore it, since it is large,
144	  regenerable, and not what you reason about. The extracted raw record — the site's own object,
145	  before any of your normalization — is **committed**, and is the durable source of truth. That
146	  split buys three things at once: re-deriving your normalized output becomes an **offline**
147	  operation, so a parser change costs no requests; the committed record doubles as the fixture
148	  for a self-test of the transform that needs no network; and a field you didn't parse this
149	  month is still there next month, because you kept the whole object rather than the subset you
150	  needed at the time.
151	
152	- **Re-running a fetch that already ran** — **fetch only what's missing**, with an explicit flag
153	  to force a refresh, so repeat runs are a no-op. Note what "resumable" is measured against: the
154	  file on disk. On a CI runner that file is durable only once the job's commit step pushes it,
155	  so a resumable script still loses everything if the runner itself dies. Chunk the work if that
156	  matters.
157	
158	- **Scheduling the refresh** — give each field its own pass on the clock it actually moves on.
159	  The single biggest cost saving in a scraper is noticing that some fields are fixed once
160	  published, some gain rows daily and some move hourly: re-fetching everything on the fastest
161	  clock re-learns a static field nightly, thousands of requests for the same answer, and it is
162	  the part of your traffic most likely to get you blocked.
163	
164	- **Generating the artifacts downstream of the stored data** — make them a **pure function of
165	  the stored master**: refresh writes to the master, and everything else regenerates from it.
166	  Files whose inputs didn't change come back byte-identical and never enter the commit, so the
167	  diff of a scheduled run is exactly what actually moved.
168

1	---
2	name: map-a-data-source
3	description: Reconnaissance on a website you want data from but don't control — locate the real data surface (hydration blob, client API, or markup) and write the findings down before any parser exists. Use when adding a new source to a scraper, or when an existing source stops parsing and you suspect the site changed shape.
4	---
5	
6	# Map a data source before you parse it
7	
8	This runs **once per source** (and again when a site is redesigned). Its output is
9	not code — it is a committed reference doc plus one saved raw payload. Everything
10	after it is ordinary parsing. The standing rules for the pipeline that follows live
11	in [the `web-scraping` pack's RULES.md](../../RULES.md).
12	
13	## 1. Fetch one page and look at what came back
14	
15	Save the raw response of a single representative page to disk and read it. You are
16	answering one question: **is the data in this document?**
17	
18	- If the interesting rows are present in the markup, you have a server-rendered page
19	  — go to step 2.
20	- If you got a small shell (a few KB of script tags and an empty root), the page is a
21	  single-page app and the data arrives separately — go to step 3.
22	
23	## 2. Look for a hydration blob first
24	
25	A server-rendered app framework almost always embeds the exact object it rendered
26	from in a script tag with a stable id. Search the saved document for a large inline
27	JSON payload and find the path to the record you want (it is usually nested a few
28	levels under a props/data wrapper).
29	
30	If one exists, **this is the surface**: it is the site's own typed record, one regex
31	and one JSON parse away, and it does not care about the layout. Save that object,
32	verbatim, as your first committed fixture.
33	
34	If there is no blob, the page's self-describing metadata (JSON-LD `<script
35	type="application/ld+json">`, `og:` meta tags) is the next-best target — it survives
36	redesigns that break element selectors.
37	
38	## 3. Find the client API
39	
40	Identify the request the page makes for its rows. Two ways in, and the second one
41	matters more than it sounds:
42	
43	- **Watch the page load** in browser devtools and read the request: URL, method,
44	  headers, auth, and the response shape.
45	- **Read the site's own JavaScript bundles.** Fetch the page, extract the script
46	  `src` paths (mind any asset prefix — the paths in the HTML already carry it),
47	  download them, and search for the operation names, query documents and field
48	  selections. For a GraphQL client the embedded query strings unescape into readable
49	  SDL, giving you the **complete** set of operations and fields the client was built
50	  against — the authoritative surface, short of introspection.
51	
52	  This path is worth knowing because it needs **only the public site host**. When the
53	  API host is blocked from where you are but the site itself loads, reading its
54	  bundle still tells you exactly what a request would look like. It cannot execute
55	  anything, so it is not a bypass of the block.
56	
57	Then note the auth story. A public listing is frequently reachable with anonymous
58	credentials the client itself ships — the same read access every visitor has. If
59	reaching the data requires a real account, stop and take that to the owner.
60	
61	## 4. Probe the shape, not just the happy path
62	
63	Before declaring the surface mapped, ask these of it explicitly, because each one has
64	silently corrupted a pipeline that assumed otherwise:
65	
66	- **Are timestamps UTC or local?** Take one item whose real-world time you can verify
67	  independently and check.
68	- **Which field is authoritative for state?** If there is both a status enum and a
69	  summarizing boolean, find an item where they disagree — there usually is one.
70	- **What are the enum's legal values?** Take them from the service's own options
71	  endpoint, not from the sample you happened to pull.
72	- **Are numbers numbers?** Amounts and counts frequently arrive as strings.
73	- **Is anything missing from this surface entirely?** A listing endpoint often
74	  carries flags but no amounts, with the real values behind a separate per-item
75	  query. Find that out now, not after you've shipped a catalogue of nulls.
76	- **Is there a bulk form?** If the per-item query has no list variant, check whether
77	  one *request* can still carry many items (GraphQL aliases, a multi-id parameter).
78	
79	## 5. Write it down, then stop
80	
81	Commit a reference doc beside the scripts holding: the endpoint(s) and auth, the
82	field surface, the enum values, each answer from step 4, and — explicitly — the
83	questions you could **not** answer and where they'd have to come from. State the
84	access constraint too: which hosts are reachable from where, and which sanctioned job
85	is allowed to do the fetching.
86	
87	The bar: **a later session should be able to write the parser from this doc without
88	touching the live service.** If it can't, the reconnaissance isn't finished.
89

1	# Web Speech APIs
2	
3	Portable, project-agnostic practices for browser voice I/O — speech-to-text
4	(`webkitSpeechRecognition` / the Web Speech `SpeechRecognition` API) and
5	text-to-speech (`chrome.tts` / `speechSynthesis`) — true for any app that reads
6	or listens through the browser, read cold. These are runtime browser-behaviour
7	gotchas, knowledge you carry into the code rather than state a tool can read off
8	the repo.
9	
10	> Some of these APIs (`chrome.tts`) are extension-only; where a rule touches
11	> MV3 service-worker / content-script mechanics, only the speech-API facet is
12	> here — the general extension gotcha underneath is not.
13	
14	## Speech-to-text (`webkitSpeechRecognition` / Web Speech API)
15	
16	- **The recognizer owns its own microphone capture — you cannot hand it
17	  `getUserMedia` audio constraints.** `echoCancellation` / `noiseSuppression` /
18	  `autoGainControl` are `getUserMedia` *microphone* constraints, and the recognizer
19	  exposes no hook to set them on its internal stream (Chrome applies its default
20	  echo cancellation there regardless). To *warm* the device with a known processing
21	  state — and to read back whether echo cancellation actually engaged — run a
22	  separate preflight `getUserMedia({ audio: {…} })` capture and stop its tracks.
23	  (`suppressLocalAudioPlayback` /
24	  `restrictOwnAudio` are `getDisplayMedia` *screen-capture* constraints and have no
25	  bearing on a mic — don't reach for them here.)
26	- **Read the whole n-best list, not just alternative `[0]`.** Set
27	  `maxAlternatives` > 1 and iterate `result[0..length]` for `{ transcript,
28	  confidence }`; the ranked alternatives are exactly where homophone / near-miss
29	  recovery lives.
30	- **`onresult`, `onend`, and `onerror` all fire — settle the cycle exactly once.**
31	  Guard a `settled` flag: interim results arrive before the final one, a cycle can
32	  end with no result at all (treat `onend`-without-result as `no-speech`), and an
33	  error and an end can both arrive.
34	- **With `interimResults` off, engines omit `isFinal` — treat a result as final
35	  unless `isFinal === false`.** Don't test `if (result.isFinal)` (it's `undefined`
36	  on those engines and you'll drop every result); test `result.isFinal !== false`.
37	- **The classic recognizer streams audio to a cloud service (Google's) — plan for
38	  it.** A `network` error means "offline / service unreachable", and audio leaves
39	  the machine. On-device recognition is opt-in and capability-gated: probe
40	  `SpeechRecognition.available({ langs, processLocally: true }) === 'available'`
41	  once and cache it, set `recognizer.processLocally = true`, and **never trigger a
42	  language-pack download** (only `'available'` counts, not `'downloadable'`). When
43	  the local path is absent, fall back to ordinary cloud recognition unchanged.
44	- **Contextual biasing (`SpeechRecognitionPhrase` + `recognizer.phrases`) works
45	  only on the on-device path** — gate it behind that same availability probe and
46	  apply it best-effort (any failure falls back to un-biased recognition rather than
47	  breaking the listen cycle). Only bias **closed vocabularies you control**
48	  (a command lexicon, known labels, a spelling alphabet) with **modest** boosts:
49	  over-boosting makes the recognizer hear a biased phrase when the user actually
50	  said a same-sounding free-form utterance.
51	- **Map the raw Web Speech error names to a small taxonomy** — `not-allowed` /
52	  `service-not-allowed` → permission-denied, plus `no-speech`, `network`,
53	  `aborted`, `audio-capture`, else `other`. In particular `aborted` is the
54	  *self-inflicted* stop (you called `recognizer.abort()`), so the caller should
55	  ignore it rather than surface it as a failure.
56	- **A missed endpoint mid-utterance needs a pause watchdog, not just `onend`.**
57	  If interim hypotheses exist but no final arrives, the engine may have lost the
58	  endpoint; a timer that fires after a pause discards the half-heard input and
59	  reopens a fresh cycle (preventing "heart heart" doubles when the user repeats
60	  themselves). Set the threshold **well above a natural mid-command thinking
61	  pause** — a tight window (~1.2 s) cuts real commands; a wider one (~1.8 s) keeps
62	  only the genuine missed-endpoint case.
63	- **Mic permission is per-origin, and the grant belongs to whatever page the
64	  recognizer runs in.** In a content script the prompt reads as the *host site*
65	  asking and the grant persists for that origin. Surface it in a controlled moment:
66	  preflight `navigator.permissions.query({ name: 'microphone' })`, then a one-time
67	  `getUserMedia` to raise the prompt. **Retry the capture bare** (`{ audio: true }`)
68	  if the first constrained call is rejected — a browser balking at the constraint
69	  *shape* must not be misread as a permission denial; only a second failure is a
70	  real "denied".
71	
72	## Text-to-speech (`chrome.tts` / `speechSynthesis`)
73	
74	- **Prefer `chrome.tts` over `speechSynthesis` — it's immune to page
75	  autoplay / user-activation gating.** `speechSynthesis` invoked from a content
76	  script is subject to the host page's autoplay policy and can silently refuse to
77	  speak; `chrome.tts` (extension-only, needs the `"tts"` permission, usable from the
78	  service worker) is not. Make `chrome.tts` primary and `speechSynthesis` the
79	  fallback for non-extension document contexts.
80	- **`chrome.tts` doesn't exist in a content script — relay speak/cancel to the
81	  service worker over a port.** Keep the same `speak()`/`cancel()` contract on both
82	  sides; the in-page port sends `{ speak }` / `{ cancel }` messages and the worker
83	  drives `chrome.tts`. On port disconnect, resolve every pending `speak()` promise
84	  so a dead worker never leaves the caller awaiting an utterance that will never
85	  finish.
86	- **Voice lists load lazily — an empty `getVoices()` means "not ready yet", not
87	  "no voices".** Resolve the preferred voice on the *first* `speak()` and don't
88	  cache an empty result: fall back to the default that turn and try to resolve
89	  again next turn.
90	- **Don't trust the OS/browser default voice — it's often the most robotic one
91	  installed.** Keep an ordered list of preferred voice names, take the first one
92	  actually installed, and fall back to the default only when none match.
93	- **Resolve a `speak()` promise on *any* terminal event, and never reject.** For
94	  `chrome.tts` that's `end` / `interrupted` / `cancelled` / `error`; for
95	  `speechSynthesis` it's `onend` / `onerror`. Resolving (not rejecting) on error
96	  keeps a spoken-prompt sequence from deadlocking on one bad utterance. Use
97	  `enqueue: false` so a new line interrupts the current one for turn-taking rather
98	  than stacking up.
99	- **Neither engine reliably supports SSML — you can't force intonation.** If a
100	  punctuation cue matters (a question's rising tone), speak the cue in words
101	  ("question mark") rather than relying on prosody the engine may not apply.
102

1	# Claudinite — the canon's own non-portable working rules
2	
3	Lessons specific to working on the canon itself. Anything true for repos beyond this one belongs in
4	the shared canon under `packs/`/`skills/` instead. The `growth-extract` task appends here, each
5	lesson at the strongest mechanism available — a check where the rule is deterministic, else prose.
6	
7	## Standing owner decisions — settled, do not re-litigate
8	
9	- **Wanting a rule about what the `packs/` tree may reference** — declare and configure the
10	  `barriers` pack, extending it generically if a capability is missing. Never write standalone
11	  code that checks packs-tree segregation.
12	
13	- **Writing a `docs/<initiative>/DESIGN.md`** — the end state and its rationale only, with
14	  alternatives and their drawbacks; never requests, prior-state narrative, or owner opinions.
15	  The migration is work, not a document: its phased plan, status and remaining work live in the
16	  tracking issue (`writing-migration-plans`), never in a sibling `MIGRATION.md`.
17	
18	- **A `docs/<initiative>/DESIGN.md` whose system is now built** — its content duplicates the
19	  module headers and pack `README.md`s that must independently state the same facts once the
20	  pipeline exists, so a design doc that survives the build only has to be kept in sync with both.
21	  Verify each section actually lives there before touching anything; move what has no other
22	  home (an owner-decision record with its rationale is typically the one irreplaceable part),
23	  sweep every `§`-numbered pointer into a pack-README reference (or drop it where the sentence
24	  only cited itself), and delete the doc whole rather than trim it. Don't extend the sweep to a
25	  design doc that still describes work in flight, or a much larger one many module headers cite
26	  by section — decide those separately rather than discover the scale mid-run (#1169).
27	
28	- **Ending a session on unfinished work** — write the state into the tracking issue. The
29	  owner's opener is `continue work on #<n>`, so anything else is lost; never compose a hand-off
30	  prompt.
31	
32	- **Designing anything that spans repos** — split it: a self-contained per-repo half in the
33	  canon, the aggregation half as a Shepherd fleet task. No repo list exists anywhere in canon
34	  code; Shepherd enumerates members at runtime. A derived fleet artifact lands there as a daily
35	  auto-merged PR of a `GENERATED` file, never a commit to its `main`.
36	
37	- **Choosing a value right for nearly every project** — keep it in the pack's own code: ask
38	  nothing at adoption, write nothing into the member's config. Read config as optional — an
39	  unset key means the default, never "misconfigured".
40	
41	- **Needing a member to flip a platform setting or hold a wider credential** — last resort:
42	  per-repo manual work reliably does not happen, and the capability then dies silently in every
43	  repo nobody configured. Prefer the route that works with the Action's own `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and
44	  neutralise a blocking platform behaviour's *effect* rather than asking for the platform to be
45	  reconfigured. Where nothing weaker can work (`FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN`), name the exact scope and
46	  have the automation report when it is missing rather than degrade silently.
47	
48	- **Landing a change to what members receive** — force delivery in the same session only when
49	  *"will it work on every repo?"* is a live question: the answer turns on how members differ —
50	  engine flow, a contract their own files must satisfy, a stub or workflow, a migration record, a
51	  new config key. Then drive Shepherd's `fleet-baseline` with `follow`, report per member unasked,
52	  and attach the repos that verification needs rather than offering to; a dispatch is not a result,
53	  and 204 means queued. Where the change is uniform by construction — prose, a doc, a move of
54	  something nothing executes from the mount — the nightly converge *is* the delivery, and forcing
55	  buys noise rather than assurance.
56	
57	- **Retiring a field, option or module** — `@deprecated` on its definition, plus a comment at
58	  each sanctioned holdout's declaration site saying why it still carries the field. Never a
59	  bespoke conformance check for a deprecation. Keep the contract validating the lingering field.
60	
61	- **Wanting a `.claudinite-settings.json` entry's config validated** — that is a real JSON Schema
62	  the file points at with `$schema`, checked by ordinary tooling. Never a coded per-pack
63	  validation vocabulary or a bespoke `configSchema` type system on the manifest — built and
64	  reverted in #919 ("That's why we have schemas").
65	
66	- **Wanting to share logic between two sibling packs** — never put it in `engine/`, which breaks
67	  the package-manager model, and never make one pack depend on the other, which is what breaks
68	  pack independence. First check whether the sharing is even necessary — self-describing data
69	  (each side states its own field vocabulary) can remove the need to interpret another pack's
70	  format at all. Where identical code is still needed, consider duplicating it, possibly with a
71	  drift guard; sometimes duplication between packs is fine (#959: "why do you even need a drift
72	  guard? Just write the json. Don't overkill.").
73	
74	- **Surfacing a number a human reads as a report card** (a dashboard tile, a digest, a fleet
75	  rollup) — never a monotonic cumulative total, which says nothing about today, and never a figure
76	  nothing measures (no estimated hours saved, no score). Report a **window against the previous
77	  window**. Where a field can't be had from the reads already being made, name it as absent in the
78	  surface's own note rather than approximating it: a stated gap is information, a guess is not
79	  (owner, #1001). Before windowing a count, check whether it is built from an event log or from a
80	  point-in-time **stamp**: windowing a stamp-derived figure (e.g. "members that converged last
81	  week", counted from each member's single last-converge date) can read a steady, healthy
82	  population as declining purely from where stamps land relative to the window boundary — reserve
83	  the window-over-window shape for counts genuinely built from things that happened inside the
84	  window (#1008).
85	
86	- **Classifying an issue or work item by deriving it structurally from other live state** (a
87	  title match against what's declared at HEAD, a computed membership test) — reconsider once the
88	  derivation's own inputs can mutate while the classified object stays open. A "standing vs
89	  ad-hoc" task classification computed live from whether an issue's title matched a task declared
90	  at HEAD silently reinterpreted an open issue's own history the moment that task's frequency or
91	  name changed underneath it. An explicit marker stamped once at creation and never revisited
92	  doesn't have that failure mode — the general preference for a structural classifier over a
93	  hand-set field holds only for state that isn't itself still in flight (#1120).
94	
95	- **Scheduling the removal of a temporary compatibility tolerance** (an old-format reader, a
96	  legacy-field fallback) — gate the removal on a converge-cycle-confirmable precondition ("no
97	  member still stamps the legacy format"), never a calendar date alone. Retiring the tolerance
98	  while a member is still on the old format doesn't just leave that member behind: the value it
99	  stamps starts reading as "no version installed" to the now-stricter reader, which re-applies
100	  every migration record in the corpus (#1106).
101	
102	## Working with the owner and the session's tools
103	
104	- **Answering "why did it fail?"** — lead with the throwing call site: `file:line`, the
105	  function, and which side enforced it. A correct narrative that never names the line reads as
106	  unanswered.
107	
108	- **Reaching for `AskUserQuestion`** — it blocks for minutes (~170s median), so spend it only
109	  on a fork you cannot take back. Anything answerable from the instruction, the tree, or a
110	  reversible default: answer it, act, and say what you assumed. Never re-post a question that was
111	  declined — take its recommended default, or open the question up.
112	
113	- **Being asked to generalise something, or to review it** — land the conversions or action
114	  points it unlocks in the same change. A capability ships with the caller that exercises it; an
115	  analysis ships with the first of its recommendations applied.
116	
117	- **Calling anything on `Claude_Code_Remote`** — one call per intent, ever. Each costs
118	  minutes, and a call that returns nothing has *not* failed — the retry has run to 81% of a
119	  session's tool wall-clock. For "is it green yet" read the check status directly; to read a
120	  public sibling repo, `git clone --depth 1` (~2s), since `add_repo` attaches nothing the git
121	  proxy doesn't already serve.
122	
123	- **Waiting for something to happen** — the guard must name the condition awaited (a run's
124	  status, a file's arrival, a deadline), with no trailing padded `sleep`. A guard you wouldn't
125	  write as the *whole* test means you are sleeping and calling it polling. **Exception: GitHub
126	  CI/PR check status is not this repo's case for `Monitor` or a `curl`/shell poll loop** — this
127	  sandbox proxy-blocks `api.github.com`, so both silently report "still running" until they time
128	  out (measured ~26 minutes lost across two PRs waiting past an already-green check, #880). Read
129	  the head sha's check runs with the GitHub MCP tool instead. Poll it on a rolling backoff, or
130	  not at all when a background watcher already reports that signal.
131	
132	- **Writing a step a human must do by hand into an issue** — when asking for a manual action,
133	  make absolutely sure it is needed: a checklist whose items are mostly no-ops teaches the reader
134	  to skim it, exactly what the checklist exists to prevent. Make the breadcrumb trail a
135	  hyperlink, to the deepest existing settings URL — a link keeps working or redirects where a
136	  written-out trail goes stale the moment GitHub reorganizes the page (#952, owner-authored).
137	
138	- **Replying to an owner comment that raises more than one claim** — answer **every** claim in
139	  that first reply, including the one you intend to push back on. A claim left silently
140	  unaddressed, even when the rest of the reply is right, just makes the owner re-raise it later
141	  (#864: a placement objection went unanswered for 55 minutes before the owner repeated it).
142	
143	- **Repeating a design doc's stated architectural rationale** — verify each of its claimed
144	  grounds against the current code (declared secrets, executor permissions) before reciting it
145	  again, especially once a direct challenge has already found it wrong once. The same overstated
146	  "a task structurally cannot hold this permission" argument was corrected twice in one session —
147	  once for a GitHub Pages deploy, again minutes later for a chrome-extension release — because
148	  code-work already runs inside the executor's own Action job with the permissions in question
149	  (#1069).
150	
151	- **An owner reversing a standing decision** — the fix is not answering the question that
152	  prompted it, it is finding and purging every place in the repo (docs, comments, code defaults)
153	  that still states the old decision, and recording the new one where a future session reads it
154	  before ever asserting the stale version again. One reversal (turning local scheduling on,
155	  moving `canon-curation`) had to be repeated five times before a session treated it as a
156	  durable-artifact problem rather than a one-off answer (#364).
157	
158	- **Firing `AskUserQuestion` on a vague, destructive-sounding instruction** ("remove the entire
159	  mechanism," "get rid of the whole thing") — scope the question to pin down the boundary of the
160	  vague noun itself, not just the downstream consequences of one reading of it. A question that
161	  asked only what happens to the one dependent check, while silently assuming "entire mechanism"
162	  meant the whole engine surface, let 15 minutes of deletion, test-authoring and PR/issue
163	  bookkeeping land before the owner caught it nine minutes later and all of it was discarded with
164	  a hard reset (#1114).
165	
166	## Authoring packs, prose and checks
167	
168	- **Writing a paragraph that explains how a mechanism works** — not into a pack's `RULES.md`,
169	  which every session in every declaring repo pays for. Behaviour belongs in the module header and
170	  the pack `README.md`; the test is whether an agent could act differently for having read it.
171	
172	- **Having a deferred direction, blocked proposal or status to record** — put it in `docs/`
173	  and point at it from the issue or PR, not from a pack file: `docs/` is outside the vendor set.
174	
175	- **Naming a new canon pack** — kebab-case, named for the surface it serves rather than the
176	  first feature you are building for it. A pack whose subject is a **Claudinite feature itself**,
177	  rather than a technology or a way of working, carries the `claudinite-` prefix
178	  (`claudinite-lifecycle`, `claudinite-growth`, `claudinite-dashboard`) — owner, 2026-08-18.
179	  The directory name is the pack's public id, spelled in
180	  every member's declaration, so another casing costs a fleet-wide rename. `claudinite-growth`
181	  is grandfathered. (convertible → prose-to-checks)
182	
183	- **Starting a new Claudinite-facing capability** (a tool, a dashboard, anything meant to reach
184	  more than the current repo) — decide **which distribution model it is** before writing the
185	  first file: a member-local tool, always-on engine code, or an opt-in pack with its own
186	  adoption/scaffolding. Nothing prompts this choice on its own, and getting it wrong costs a full
187	  move-and-rewrite cycle per correction — one session paid it three times in a row before landing
188	  on "opt-in pack" (#934).
189	
190	- **Looking for a skill and not finding it in `.claude/skills/`** — read
191	  `packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` out of the tracked tree. Mounting filters on the *literal*
192	  declaration and the home doesn't declare `git-github`, so an unmounted skill says nothing about
193	  whether its procedure applies.
194	
195	- **Adding or changing a check** — update the pack's catalog row, and re-run the suite against
196	  current `main` before merging: a whole-tree aggregate is judged post-merge, so a branch's own green
197	  never covers it. Never transcribe a corpus-wide total into a doc — `packs/README.md` states how to
198	  count checks and rules instead of quoting a number, so every pack change no longer edits it.
199	  (portable → `merge-to-main`)
200	
201	- **Writing a check's `fix` text** — name only remedies that match the enforced severity;
202	  sessions follow the words, not the `severity` field. An advisory finding's remedies are act on
203	  it or leave it, never a config-acceptance escape.
204	
205	- **Declaring a check, or adding a key to the vocabulary** — name the key so the declaration
206	  reads alone to someone who hasn't read the design doc (`scanFiles`, `matchLines`,
207	  `relevantWhen`): if it needs a comment to be read, it needs a better name. Declarations live in
208	  `packs/<pack>/declared-checks.json`, which cannot hold one, and borrow nothing from prose — no
209	  `description`, no `doc`; the line the agent reads is `failureMessage`.
210	
211	- **Writing a check that reads the session transcript** — screen the harness's own **plain-text**
212	  pseudo-turns, not only the tag-wrapped ones. `humanText` in
213	  `engine/checks/helpers/session-transcript.mjs` drops a user entry that starts with `<`, which
214	  lets a bracketed marker straight through: `comment-classification` blocked a session on
215	  `[Request interrupted by user for tool use]` as "the owner's latest comment". A conversation rule
216	  fires at the Stop hook, where a false positive spends a whole cycle on something no edit can
217	  clear — so its fixture carries an interruption marker beside a real owner turn.
218	
219	- **A doc reached only by following a link out of `RULES.md` or a check's `doc:`/`More:` line** —
220	  if it is a how-to wanted at authoring time rather than prose every session should carry, convert
221	  it into a skill (frontmatter + description) invocable by description, not a doc chained through
222	  links nobody follows cold (#975).
223	
224	- **A check declaration's `doc:` field** — nothing ever opens it; it only renders into a finding's
225	  `More:` line when the check actually fires. A stale pointer left by a file move can sit broken
226	  indefinitely with nothing to catch it — grep for and re-verify every `doc:` field by hand
227	  whenever you move or rename the file it points at (#975).
228	
229	- **A check built to catch a thing being missing or misnamed** — don't gate the check's own
230	  relevance on the single signal it exists to validate. Gating solely on "does the orchestrating
231	  file still have the expected name" makes the exact failure the check exists to catch (a rename)
232	  also the thing that silences the check — the run that should say "rename it back" never fires.
233	  Use two independent signals, either sufficient, so at least one survives when the other is the
234	  thing that broke (#1060).
235	
236	- **Deciding whether an enforced check still earns its keep** — measure its actual blocking-firing
237	  rate against what it buys, not vibes. A check whose firings are dominated by cases where the
238	  agent had already done the right thing, and the check only wants the exact tokens for it, is a
239	  demotion candidate (check → prose-only), justified by the firing-frequency data itself:
240	  `comment-classification` fired 204 times in 31 days, 21% of all blocking findings, each one a
241	  blocked Stop-hook turn spent re-emitting a line the session had already been told to emit
242	  (#1118).
243	
244	- **A documented multi-step procedure the agent re-derives interactively every time it runs** —
245	  that pattern, not the doc's polish, is the signal to mechanize it into a script the agent runs
246	  once. A nine-part prose bootstrap doc cost ~90 exploratory tool calls and ~11 minutes per
247	  adoption for work that runs in seconds once scripted. Part of that cost was sequencing, not
248	  exploration: the tracking issue was created only after the first commit had already failed the
249	  issue-reference check, costing a full amend/force-push/CI cycle — create the artifact a check
250	  will demand *before* the action it gates, not after (#1132).
251	
252	## The engine, the mount and what reaches members
253	
254	- **Writing a path, regex or command against the mount** — write the two-root form: the
255	  `.claudinite/(shared|local)/` prefix optional in a pattern, and a probe for
256	  `.claudinite/shared/` falling back to the repo root. The home runs the same code from the repo
257	  root, so a mount-shaped path works fleet-wide and fails on exactly this repo — where it
258	  surfaces last.
259	
260	- **Adding a module under `packs/`** — keep it import-light, and start work after evaluation
261	  completes (`check(…).catch(…)`), never in a top-level `await`. Discovery imports every
262	  `pack.mjs` and `checks.mjs` before activation is consulted, so a module that is also a CLI entry
263	  point is re-imported mid-evaluation and Node exits 13 having run nothing.
264	  `pack-discovery-entry-await` enforces the await half only.
265	
266	- **Tightening a contract that member-owned files must satisfy** — first ask what carries it
267	  across the fleet. Vendoring refreshes `.claudinite/shared/` only and a migration record moves
268	  paths, not schemas — so if the answer is "nothing", accept the legacy shape in
269	  `normalizeManifest` until a carrier exists. Never let a stale declaration degrade to *fewer
270	  checks running* rather than a failure.
271	
272	- **Renaming a pack whose config a member writes into their own repo** — the rename map fixes
273	  code-side id resolution, but it cannot rewrite a member's own already-committed config, which
274	  converges on its own separate schedule or never. A reader consuming that config keeps resolving
275	  both the new key and every legacy spelling explicitly and permanently: rewriting the write side
276	  to the new name (the fix for the fleet's own persisted data) only helps where the engine itself
277	  owns the write, not data a member wrote into their own repo (#1081).
278	
279	- **Checking whether an actor may trigger a privileged automated action off a GitHub issue/PR
280	  payload** — read the actor's permission from the collaborators-permission API
281	  (`GET /repos/{o}/{r}/collaborators/{u}/permission`), never the payload's `author_association`:
282	  `MEMBER` covers any org member regardless of repo permission, and `COLLABORATOR` includes
283	  read-only collaborators — both broader than push access (#1067).
284	
285	- **Extending what a copied stub reads** — make the new config key optional, fail the run when
286	  it is declared-but-unset, and let declaring it trigger a staleness check (`build_vars` /
287	  `release-workflows` is the shape). Stubs are copied into a member's `.github/` once and never
288	  re-copied, so a new key is silently dead in every repo holding the old copy.
289	
290	- **Writing a migration record that needs engine behaviour newer than itself** — have
291	  `appliesTo` probe the member's own mount for that capability, by content rather than version,
292	  and stay inert until it reads back; an unreadable mount must read as "not capable". The record
293	  comes from a fresh canon clone but the worker executing it is the member's vendored one, so
294	  otherwise the converge fails, the mount never advances, and the fix can never arrive.
295	
296	- **Changing an export in `updates/*`** — empty it, never remove it. Fielded workers are stale
297	  callers of instantly-current flow modules, so a removal wedges every member permanently on its
298	  next run. Keep it callable, say at its definition that this is why, and pin the surface with a
299	  test carrying an expiry — the canary rehearsal cannot catch this class, since it drives the
300	  worker this ref ships. Retire it by reading the field: the condition is that no member's
301	  *vendored* worker calls it.
302	
303	- **Renaming or deleting an `engine/` module a `packs/` file imports** — leave a shim at the old
304	  path re-exporting what it named, for the same reason and by the same rule as `updates/*` above:
305	  the engine lane and the pack lane deliver in separate PRs on separate cycles, and pack delivery is
306	  version-gated per pack, so every member spends a window holding the NEW engine beside an OLD pack.
307	  The failure is worse than a broken task — a pack that fails to load fails the mount's self-test,
308	  the converge then refuses to land AT ALL, and the member cannot receive the pack version that
309	  would have fixed it (#1004: a green run, an unmoved stamp, and a `needs-human` PR). Ask which
310	  symbols are fielded by walking the TRUNK's pack history, never `--all` — an import that only ever
311	  existed on an unmerged branch is not fielded, and scanning every ref fires on whatever is in
312	  flight.
313	
314	- **Changing a vendored stub** — edit the canon's own `.github/workflows/` copy in the same
315	  commit and diff the two whole files. The canon has no converge, so its copy drifts invisibly
316	  until it is a permission denial in production.
317	
318	- **Excluding files from the vendor set by pattern** — whitelist any operational file that
319	  matches by path, and pin it with a test against the real canon tree, not only a fixture. The
320	  nightly refresh re-runs the computation from canon HEAD, so a bug there is the one canon
321	  regression that is not self-healing. Assert that the **whole containing directory** vendors,
322	  not just the one file that broke — a test re-asserting only the known-missing file needs a
323	  fresh edit for the next file added there; one that walks the real directory doesn't (#907).
324	
325	- **Retiring or reshaping a protocol the engine exposes** (a dispatch input, a stub's declared
326	  interface) — sweep for callers **outside this repo**, not just what greps locally. `FORCE_TASKS`'s
327	  replacement broke Shepherd's only caller because the migration enumerated this repo's own
328	  callers and missed the cross-repo one (#929); two independently-maintained stub copies at the
329	  same path declaring different input names is the same failure from the other side (#801, #907)
330	  — the two spellings *are* the protocol, and they live in different trees.
331	
332	- **Branching on the result of an API write in fleet machinery** — read its status, not just
333	  the body: a body-only destructure turns a 403 into a plausible object and the run still logs
334	  `ok`. Judge the fleet by members' stamps, never by run conclusions — the stamp is the only
335	  artifact that moves when delivery actually worked.
336	
337	- **A single timeout bound covering two different waits** ("has this even started" vs. "is
338	  something already running about to finish") reintroduces the bug a prior fix closed, on
339	  whichever side crosses the shorter phase's real need. Split the bound to match what each phase
340	  is actually waiting on, sized from that work's own declared budget rather than a round number —
341	  and once a bound is hit, the give-up message must never read as a verdict on the work: "no
342	  successful run yet" is a statement about the clock, not about the runs, and collapsing the two
343	  sent a reader chasing a wrong repository-settings diagnosis for CI that was simply still running
344	  (#1027).
345	
346	- **Writing generated content into a size-capped GitHub API field** (an issue or PR body) —
347	  budget it explicitly, in two tiers: an always-complete compact summary plus best-effort detail
348	  rationed to a byte budget with an explicit omitted-count, never a single unbounded write that
349	  can 422 outright at the ~64KB cap. `growth-dedup`'s brief rendered 350KB against that limit and
350	  would have failed the run at its first step.
351	
352	- **Writing a generated title whose naive content scales with a variable-length list** (a PR
353	  title, a notification headline) — collapse the list to a count and keep the per-item detail in
354	  the body. A title is a summary surface, not a second body, and grows unreadable exactly where a
355	  long list makes every character compete for space (#1048).
356	
357	- **Preflighting a required grant or permission** — a probe is only as good as the environment it
358	  runs against; where the failure is conditional (a scope that 403s only under a specific
359	  condition, e.g. a private repo), a probe run where that condition isn't met reports a
360	  false-positive pass. Prefer attributing a real observed 403 to the permission that would fix it
361	  over guessing from an unrepresentative probe (#1052).
362	
363	- **Introducing a finer-grained classification of an existing catch-all state** — default
364	  whatever an older or unaware writer produces (or a future writer's not-yet-known category) to
365	  the most conservative member of the new set, not the most lenient. An unlabelled park now reads
366	  as the blocking `failure` lane rather than a soft one, so a writer that predates the split fails
367	  safe instead of silently landing in a lane nobody watches (#1051).
368	
369	- **Adding a fleet task** — fail loudly on a Context target it cannot reach rather than
370	  proceeding on a partial list, and treat a member as un-adopted until the routine's repo scope
371	  names it. The target list is enumerated over `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` while the grant is hand-typed
372	  UI config no Action can read; the drift *completes*, filing a report that reads as a full sweep.
373	
374	- **Spawning a child process from a worker** — pass an explicit `cwd`, resolved to a root that
375	  cannot vanish (`--root`, then `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`, then `cwd`). The converge deletes the tree
376	  its own code-work runs inside, so children die at `process.cwd()` before doing anything. Keep
377	  "could not run" distinguishable from "had nothing to run": a crash sharing a benign outcome code
378	  is unobservable.
379	
380	- **Diagnosing a member's maintenance PR that won't land** — `unstable` beside a green sweep
381	  is a parked `action_required` run, not a missing repo setting. Read the member's raw
382	  `.claudinite-settings.json` and the head sha's `pull_request` runs; propose a platform-settings
383	  change only as a conclusion, never as a diagnosis.
384	
385	- **Judging whether a member is fresh** — read its `ref` (or `engineVersion` /
386	  `packVersions`), never `claudinite.updated` alone: a held stamp pins `updated` behind a pending
387	  note, so a mount converging hourly can look a week stale.
388	
389	- **Reading a uniform signal across every fleet member right after a shared mechanism changes**
390	  — a rate-limited, unauthenticated `api.github.com` probe can return a clean-looking uniform
391	  negative across every target, and a uniform stamp/ref shared by the whole fleet can mean "not
392	  yet past its nightly anchor" rather than "frozen." Check for a rate-limit signal explicitly
393	  before trusting a uniform empty sweep, and check timing — has each member's own convergence
394	  window actually passed — before generalizing one member's confirmed fault to the fleet. Never
395	  reuse a signal already known unreliable to corroborate a different theory (#801, #939: a "the
396	  entire fleet is frozen" claim stood uncorrected for ~10 hours).
397	
398	- **Retiring or migrating a dispatch/config parameter channel** — a parameter that stops being
399	  read must fail loudly, never silently default. A dropped safety knob (e.g. `DRY_RUN`) defaults
400	  to the operation's *most dangerous* mode — live, unscoped — not a safe one; audit that a
401	  parameter's producer and consumer still agree after every interface migration (#974,
402	  owner-authored).
403	
404	- **Relying on a push to trigger further Actions workflows** — a push authored with the default
405	  `GITHUB_TOKEN` (which every converge and auto-merge in this repo's own machinery uses) fires no
406	  `on: push` workflow; only a push carrying a real user or app credential cascades. A dashboard
407	  stuck showing a stale "hasn't converged" banner traced back to exactly this: the deploy
408	  workflow's trigger never fired for the pushes that actually moved a mount (#1094). The same
409	  platform fact is why `.github/workflows/` is the one path a converge cannot push into — it lands
410	  only through a PR a human merges — so a renamed or removed entry point that a workflow file
411	  references by literal path needs a shim held open until every consumer's own copy has moved, by
412	  the same rule as an `engine/` module a `packs/` file imports (#1108).
413	
414	- **A script written for one execution context silently breaking in another** — audit every
415	  script's environment assumptions (a real `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `gh`/`curl` reachability) whenever the
416	  execution context of its caller changes, not just at the one call site that surfaced the break.
417	  A script written when the queue ran as an Actions job (a real token, shell GitHub access) 401'd
418	  once the same work started running inside an agent session (MCP-only, a proxy-scoped token, no
419	  `gh`) — and per the owner, every other script built against the old assumption fails identically
420	  in the new context, not just the one that broke first (#1133).
421	
422	- **Finding a check that watches only one of two structurally-identical surfaces** — widen it to
423	  the sibling in the same change rather than filing it separately. A check exercising the
424	  scheduler's own vendored stub had never been extended to the executor's stub, which is just as
425	  much a fleet-wide vendored surface and just as capable of drifting unnoticed (#1138).
426	
427	- **Picking a compact date-encoded identifier** (a version stamp, a compact timestamp) — check
428	  the encoding's own rollover boundary years ahead, not just today's decode correctness: anchoring
429	  a year on its last digit wraps to 0 in 2030 and sorts a decade of releases underneath every 2029
430	  one, so the anchor point matters (`year - 2020`, not `year % 10`). And keep the identifier
431	  string-typed everywhere it travels — `'60820.10'` and `'60820.1'` are different versions and the
432	  same float, so nothing in the corpus may parse one as a number (#1105).
433	
434	- **Designing text that instructs a model to echo an exact string** (a session-start directive, a
435	  generated title) — don't reference the payload anaphorically from later text ("that line," "the
436	  above"); state the instruction first, have it disclaim itself as instruction-not-payload, and
437	  put the literal string once, last, introduced by the instruction's own colon. Recency is what an
438	  LLM actually resolves ambiguous reference against: putting the directive *after* the payload
439	  line made "that line" read as the directive sentence itself, and a session opened two replies in
440	  a row reciting the instruction verbatim instead of the summary (#1126).
441	
442	- **A work-scope check that verifies "this PR bumped X" by diffing against `main`** — on a PR
443	  stacked on another still-open one, that diff already carries the lower PR's own bump, so the
444	  check reads it as *this* PR's and passes green even though this PR's own edits still need one.
445	  The false green survives only until the lower PR merges and this one rebases onto the real
446	  base. Re-verify (and re-bump if needed) after every earlier PR in the stack actually lands —
447	  never trust a stacked PR's check result against its pre-merge base (`pack-version-bumped`,
448	  #1119).
449	
450	## Scheduled tasks
451	
452	- **Choosing a task's cadence** — take it from how often the signal actually moves. A
453	  precondition reading `sharedMount` fires nearly every night and spends an opus session on it;
454	  where the work isn't latency-sensitive, daily buys noise, not freshness, and a weekly run still
455	  sees all 7 days because a task's signal window is its OWN period plus an hour of slack.
456	
457	- **After any scheduler-mechanism flip** (how forced/manual work is dispatched, how a
458	  precondition is evaluated) — re-audit every task whose precondition assumed the old mechanism.
459	  A stale `run: false` that was previously "consulted by nothing" becomes a live self-closing
460	  landmine under the new mechanism — the third instance of this exact class in this repo (#929,
461	  #921, #971); grep for `frequency: 'manual'` plus its precondition text, not just the flipped
462	  mechanism's own callers.
463	
464	- **Writing a task's precondition** — gate on the objects' own movement in the window (a
465	  `touched` list, a tip-commit date the collector actually carries), never on standing state,
466	  which is true forever once true. A signal true most days — a substantive `main` move — may
467	  only *widen* an already-triggered run. The gate is not the scope: where a verdict is relative to
468	  the rest of the set, newness gates and the full set stays the scope. (portable →
469	  `claudinite-growth/skills/writing-tasks/SKILL.md`)
470	
471	- **Writing a task whose output is a regenerated file** — land it through
472	  `engine/scheduler/deliver-generated.mjs` and read its prior state from the fetched base, not
473	  local HEAD. One executor run drains several items from one checkout, so a worker that checks out
474	  a branch or leaves an index behind hands the next item a tree it did not expect.
475	  (`basics/baselining` is the deliberate exception.)
476	
477	- **Wanting to exercise a task Action-side** — dispatch the scheduler workflow with its `wake`
478	  input naming the task, which clears the standing item's wait and puts it back in the queue; the
479	  post-scheduler run drain then picks it up in the same run. The precondition is still evaluated at pickup,
480	  so a wake that finds no work SAYS so on the item — a forced run that does nothing is a verdict,
481	  not a failure. (Under the retired slot scheduler this did not work at all: dueness was stateless,
482	  so an off-window `workflow_dispatch` printed `- no tasks due` and looked exactly like a healthy
483	  run.)
484	
485	- **Converging an unattended run** — do the final label/comment/close sequence as the run's very
486	  next action once the outcome is known, not deferred to a checklist recalled from memory at the
487	  end of a long session, when context is fullest and the remaining work looks like formality.
488	  Two runs closed `outcome:done` while their own PR sat open needing a human, and one skipped the
489	  outcome label and the exec record entirely (#939, #892) — five days of green-looking runs on
490	  one of them. `outcome:done` means nothing is left for anyone to act on; never close it while a
491	  PR, branch, or open question from this run is still live.
492	
493	- **Decomposing a pipeline into chained tasks** — chain stages by preconditions that each
494	  re-derive the world's actual state, never by parameters or Context passed forward. A run
495	  interrupted mid-pipeline then self-heals on the next pick instead of needing `on_interrupt`
496	  handling at every stage, and `on_interrupt: 'needs-human'` narrows to the one stage whose side
497	  effect is genuinely non-idempotent (#1073).
498	
499	- **Passing a diagnostic verdict out of a subprocess that may be killed at its own timeout
500	  ceiling** — write it to the live output stream (stdout/stderr), never to a file meant to be
501	  written at exit: already-printed output survives a `SIGKILL`, a file written on the way out is
502	  never written at all if the kill lands first (#1051).
503	
504	- **Writing a stateless reconciliation or repair rule over a live, mutating collection** (a
505	  janitor sweep, a stale-item rule) — distinguish rules gated on a *clock* (elapsed time, safe
506	  against snapshot staleness) from rules gated on *current state* (need a fresh, targeted read of
507	  the specific item immediately before acting, never the snapshot that triggered the sweep). An
508	  item that settled between the sweep's read and its write is otherwise indistinguishable from a
509	  genuinely torn state machine: a claim-to-close window that had shrunk to ~4 seconds let a janitor
510	  rule stamp `task:done` and `needs-human` on an issue that had already succeeded (#1101, fixed in
511	  #1108).
512	
513	- **Solving a "must act again later" or "must verify eventually" problem** — check whether an
514	  existing generic lane already gives you everything before building new standing machinery for
515	  it. A first cut added a whole new daily task, keyed on a title-prefix scan, to handle deferred
516	  production-verification; the owner pointed at the deferred-request queue's existing
517	  `Blocked-by`/`Not-before` lane, which already carried it end to end, and the bespoke task — a
518	  second queue standing beside the first — came back out (#1092).
519	
520	- **Building a dedup or mutex over work items** — a same-title match only catches two items that
521	  are literally the same request twice; it is blind to two items that conflict by writing the
522	  same *target* (one file, one member's config) under two different titles. Two work lists on one
523	  member (`task:origin:ad-hoc`'s own REQUESTED/SUSPECTED split) hit exactly this: nothing
524	  serialized them until the enforcer named the member's other open list in `Blocked-by:`, letting
525	  the queue's own dependency field do the serializing the title mutex couldn't (#1119). Key a
526	  conflict guard on the target the write lands on, never on the requester's phrasing.
527	
528	## Proving a change
529	
530	- **Testing a change to a task's triggering** — drive the real `planSchedulerRun` from a clock at which
531	  the task's anchor has NOT come. Instantiation is decided before any precondition runs, so a test
532	  that starts from an item already in the queue proves only "works once instantiated" and says
533	  nothing about whether the occurrence is ever created.
534	
535	- **Testing a fail-soft step** — assert the positive effect (the output IS emitted), never
536	  `status === 0`, which fail-soft makes meaningless. The engine is vendored verbatim, so one such
537	  regression silently disables that step across the whole fleet.
538	
539	- **Writing a check that selects inputs by path pattern** — assert over the real tree that its
540	  scope is non-empty; a pattern left behind by a layout change matches nothing, reads as live and
541	  catches nothing, and fixtures spelling the same dead layout keep proving the matching. Likewise
542	  grep the tree for any directory you name in a finding, a remedy or a doc pointer before shipping
543	  it.
544	
545	- **Testing a helper reapplied across a hand-off, a re-queue or a retry** — call it twice and
546	  assert no duplication. A suite of single-call tests stays green while the multi-call case
547	  corrupts state. When the mechanism arbitrates by identity (a claim, a lock), the second call
548	  must come from a **different actor** — a single actor retrying its own stale claim can't expose
549	  an identity-masked race, which is exactly what hid F18 until two distinct executors raced (#925).
550	
551	- **Building or extending a simulator for a stateful engine mechanism** — model what the real
552	  engine's code actually *writes* (the artifact), never the rule's stated *intent*. A sim that
553	  advances state on every transition matching the rule's description, rather than only where the
554	  real engine leaves a mark, is correct by construction and blind to exactly the silent paths
555	  where the two diverge — which is where the bug lived (an episode-boundary livelock, #925).
556	
557	- **Asserting a mid-run invariant in a simulator or test** — capture it at the exact moment the
558	  state holds, not after the run continues past it. A check re-queued before an item had ever left
559	  a state asserted over an item that never actually failed; by the end of the run normal
560	  convergence had already cleared the evidence the assertion meant to catch (#1054).
561	
562	- **A test that derives its answer by walking git history** (which imports are still fielded, from
563	  trunk) — guard explicitly against a shallow clone and fail loudly rather than silently evaluate
564	  over whatever partial history happens to be present. A shallow checkout would otherwise let the
565	  test pass vacuously exactly when the real answer needs history it doesn't have (#1013).
566	
567	- **Restoring source after a deliberate see-it-fail mutation** — `git checkout -- <file>` (or
568	  `git stash`) at the moment of mutating, never a `.bak` copy taken earlier: a `.bak` predates
569	  whatever else you edited in between, and restoring from it silently destroys that work (#922).
570	  `git checkout --` restores from the index, so it destroys *uncommitted* work in the same file
571	  just as thoroughly. Commit or stage the real edit **before** mutating anything to see it fail,
572	  and only mutate a file whose current state you are ready to throw away (#1010).
573	
574	- **Running the test suite** — `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`. There is no test
575	  script, and every hand-written glob under-runs it silently: `node --test <dir>` doesn't recurse,
576	  and bash `**` without `globstar` reached 37 of 65 files. `ci.yml`'s array is not authoritative
577	  either. Redirect one run to a file and grep that file for whatever slice you need next — never
578	  re-run the ~55s suite to re-slice the same unchanged output (five reruns cost 4.5 minutes for
579	  five different greps, #930, #931).
580	
581	- **Iterating on a sweep across many files** — while iterating, run only the test files the edit
582	  touches plus `check_the_work`; spend the whole suite and `check_the_world` once, at the end,
583	  before the commit. Both are whole-tree aggregates whose verdict cannot turn on one file of a
584	  sweep, and re-running them per edit is what the session actually costs: of one night's tool
585	  wall-clock, the session that landed #993 spent 18 full-suite runs (18 min) and 22 world sweeps
586	  (7 min) out of 26 min, #941's spent 22 (22 min) and 27 (12 min) out of 33 min, and #992's 7 and
587	  8 out of 14 min.
588	
589	- **Surveying whether something exists in the tree** — a code-search hit is evidence; a
590	  code-search miss is not. Survey by reading each file.
591	
592	- **Documenting or relying on a named knob** (a declaration field, an env var, a config key, a
593	  counter series) — the corpus naming it is not evidence it exists: grep for the code that
594	  **reads** it and the code that **writes** it first. One window turned up all three misses.
595	  Designed and never built, documented as live: `CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL`, beside `exclusive`
596	  which had retired with its mechanism (#975). A writer with no reader left: `session_scope`, with
597	  nothing saying so (#993). And a reader with no writer left: the usage fold's `tasks` census,
598	  whose parser outlived the log lines it read, so the rows keep counting plausibly until the
599	  Actions retention window ages out and then count nothing (#994). That last shape is the one to
600	  design against — deleting a writer is the same change as marking its series historical, never
601	  something to notice later when the numbers reach zero.
602	
603	- **Writing check-the-work** — make sure you validate it fails: create the conditions that fail
604	  the check and see it go red (#966, #970).
605	
606	- **Renaming an entity** — sweep for references in code and comments, don't change historical
607	  records, and re-render generated files rather than editing them by hand (#957).
608	
609	- **Renaming a word that is also stored data** (a counter key, a wire word, a label) — the sweep
610	  is not finished at the code. A persisted aggregate holds rows keyed by the old spelling, so the
611	  **decode** side must rename them too, or the next encode writes those historical counts as
612	  `null` — silently, and only for the old rows. And on a *second* rename of one name, map every
613	  legacy spelling **straight to today's** rather than chaining one normalization onto the last, so
614	  a declaration written for the oldest vocabulary still normalizes in a single pass (#1013).
615	
616	- **Writing a "this period is covered" marker in an at-least-once or idempotent pipeline** (a
617	  watermark row, a dedup stamp) — write it strictly after the durable effect it is guarding, and
618	  never let it stand in as proof the effect happened. Modeling a decision row as sufficient cover
619	  for its period ate a real occurrence whenever the item the row promised had failed to actually
620	  get created: a write failure was silently read as "already handled," the exact inversion of the
621	  system's own fail-open policy. Caught by the simulator before any engine code shipped; the fix
622	  scopes the marker to the *declined* case only — a go verdict's coverage is judged by the item it
623	  actually created, never by the row (#1123).
624	
625	## Editing, branching and merging here
626	
627	- **Making a throwaway probe commit on a scratch branch to see a check fail** — `git commit -am`
628	  stages *every* modified file, not just the probe's own change; a subsequent `git branch -D` of
629	  that scratch branch discards any real in-progress edit it swept up along with the probe. Stash
630	  or otherwise isolate real pending edits first (#939).
631	
632	- **Editing a repo's JSON config** — patch it as anchored text; never re-serialize. A
633	  round-trip rewrites what it wasn't asked to (`ensure_ascii` escapes, indent, key order, trailing
634	  newline) while nothing fails and tests stay green. (portable → `repo-text-sweeps`) **Exception:**
635	  when the target can sit inside a nested array within an entry object (e.g. a pack's own
636	  `via`/`config` array nested inside its `{"id": …}` entry), an anchored regex cannot cross the
637	  nested closing bracket, so every element after it goes silently unreached — and a fixture built
638	  without that nesting proves nothing, since it spells the same gap the pattern has. Parse and
639	  rewrite structurally there instead, preserving key order/config/`via`/answers by hand (#1042).
640	
641	- **Returning to a branch that waited** — after `git fetch`, re-verify the *premise*, unasked:
642	  read what the new commits did to the surface you are changing and say whether the problem is
643	  still there and what survives. This repo auto-merges its own PRs on top of migrations that
644	  retire whole directories, so a branch can rebase cleanly, stay green, and no longer be the
645	  change to make.
646	
647	- **Re-verifying a branch against a `main` that has moved** — `git rebase origin/main`, never
648	  `git merge origin/main`. A merge commit trips the blocking squash-merge-history check and costs
649	  a full rebase, a discarded CI run, and a fresh wait — paid twice in one evening on #880.
650	
651	- **After a PR lands by squash-merge** — `git remote prune origin` before touching that branch
652	  again. GitHub deletes the head ref on squash-merge here, so a stale local tracking ref makes git
653	  count the pre-squash commits as unpushed: the next push is rejected and the stop hook reports
654	  phantom local work (#922).
655	
656	- **Re-applying your edit onto a moved `main`** — re-read the fetched file, apply the same
657	  anchored edit, and confirm the stat shows insertions only. A pack's `RULES.md` is append-only
658	  and written several times a day, so restoring a whole-file copy deletes those lessons and
659	  nothing goes red.
660	
661	- **Syncing local `main`** — `git fetch origin main && git reset --hard origin/main`,
662	  unconditionally. The clones are shallow, so `git pull` finds no common ancestor and reports the
663	  stale local ref as carrying unique commits; nothing of value is ever on this repo's local
664	  `main`. (portable → `git-github`)
665	
666	- **Merging in a session that also has a consumer repo in its sources** — resolve the merge
667	  skill by *target repo*, not by which skill matched first. The consumer's skill wins on name and
668	  is followed to the letter, silently skipping the canon-only steps — repeatedly the post-merge
669	  conversation capture (`node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`), which is
670	  part of the merge, not an optional epilogue.
671	
672	- **Having work that completes or corrects an open PR** — put it on that PR's branch. A
673	  dispatch prompt's designated branch routes work, not review; splitting gives the owner two gates
674	  for one decision and invites approving half.
675	
676	- **Wanting to combine two PRs** — update the one you're keeping and close the other. Never
677	  push one's branch onto the other's base: GitHub marks a PR merged as soon as its head is
678	  reachable from its base, and a later `state: closed` is a no-op. Check the API's `merged` field
679	  before reporting.
680	
681	- **Being asked "should no X decide this?"** — it questions whether the decision exists at
682	  all; never answer it by relocating the knob one rung out. Ask who would ever set it differently
683	  and why that can't be read off the structure — a single structural answer means delete the
684	  field and document the exception where it lives.
685	
686	- **Facing a retry across a call whose outcome you cannot observe** — check whether declining
687	  to retry removes the uncertainty before building dedup or arbitration machinery to manage it. A
688	  timeout is exactly the case where you cannot know the first call did nothing.
689

input.prompt:
You are helping with a task called "rule revalidation" in the Claudinite repo (a Claude Code agent-instructions framework). We are enumerating "revalidatable claims" across pack documentation and check declarations — sentences/assertions that assert a FACT ABOUT THE ENVIRONMENT that could go stale: how the Claude Code harness/tools behave, GitHub API/permission behavior, MCP tool existence/parameters/behavior, version floors, or external runtime behavior. NOT in scope: judgment/taste rules, rules about how this repo itself is organized, product requirements, anything a reviewer could verify just by reading the tree.

Part A — read these remaining RULES.md/SKILL.md files not yet covered by other batches (read each with the Read tool), and list every revalidatable claim as: file path, exact quoted sentence, one-line description of what a probe would check:
1. packs/claudinite-canary-repo/RULES.md (if it exists)
2. packs/claudinite-dashboard/RULES.md (if it exists)
3. packs/executable-requirements/RULES.md (if it exists)
4. packs/html/RULES.md (if it exists)
5. packs/ios/RULES.md (if it exists)
6. packs/leaflet/RULES.md (if it exists)
7. packs/macos/RULES.md (if it exists)
8. packs/node/RULES.md (if it exists)
9. packs/play-store-release/RULES.md (if it exists)
10. packs/python/RULES.md (if it exists)
11. packs/product-wiki/RULES.md (if it exists)
12. packs/barriers/RULES.md (if it exists)
13. .claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/RULES.md (if it exists)
Use Glob first (packs/*/RULES.md and packs/*/skills/*/SKILL.md) to find which of these actually exist plus any you missed, and read all of them. Skip files already covered above only if truly absent.

Part B — find all `packs/*/declared-checks.json` files (14 of them) via Glob, read each, and flag any check whose `failureMessage` or `fix` text asserts something about the environment (a tool's behavior, GitHub API behavior, an MCP contract) rather than purely about this repo's own file layout/conventions. List: file path, check id, the claim, what a probe would check.

Be selective — most content is judgment/process guidance or repo-internal convention, NOT a revalidatable claim. Return findings as a structured list grouped by file; say "none" for files with zero claims. Be concise — this is data for another process, not a report for a human.
