attachment.content:
- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one — Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

1	# Executable requirements — the framework standard
2	
3	The concrete conventions for running a numbered spec as tests — the mechanics only. The judgment
4	layer they implement — doc-first red-by-default, owner-owned expecteds, honest-gap tracking — is
5	not here, so a new project or a new stack adopts the framework by convention instead of
6	re-deriving it. Worked implementations: GoogleCalendarEventCreator (origin; extension/jsdom
7	rendering), TLDR (adds a cross-tier `server` kind), ShoutsAndWhispers (Flutter port; first `saga`
8	kind).
9	
10	## 1. The layout is the contract
11	
12	- Everything lives under **`dev/requirements/`**: `requirements.md` (the numbered prose spec),
13	  one **top-level folder per kind**, `shared/` for cross-kind infra, and the runners/gates. The
14	  spec file's path is the framework's structural fingerprint — this pack activates on it.
15	- **A requirement line** starts (optionally after a list dash) with a backtick-wrapped dotted
16	  number: `` `4.2` ``. A **leaf** is an id with no finer-numbered child. Parse with one shared
17	  regex (`` ^\s*(?:-\s+)?`(\d+(?:\.\d+)+)` ``) so specs stay drop-in compatible across projects.
18	- **The line is a scannable one-liner; expanded detail collapses.** A leaf in `requirements.md`
19	  reads as a single line the owner skims down the numbered spine on GitHub. Any expansion —
20	  rationale, acceptance notes, edge cases, the owner-verification recipe — lives inside a
21	  collapsed `<details>` block under the line, hidden until the owner expands it. The doc reviews
22	  as a clean spec, not walls of prose; the depth is one click away when wanted, invisible when
23	  not.
24	- **The folder is the kind.** A case's kind is the directory it lives in; the case declares no
25	  kind field. Cases are
26	  `<kind>/cases/<slug>.<leaf-id>.case.<ext>`: a stable feature slug (so retitling a spec section
27	  never forces renames), then the dotted leaf id.
28	- **Artifact expecteds live beside their case** (`<slug>.<id>.png`, `expected/<name>.json`);
29	  failure artifacts (actual/diff renders) go to a gitignored dir, never beside the goldens.
30	- Where the language discovers cases dynamically (Node `require`), the registry walks the
31	  folders; where it cannot (Dart/Flutter), each kind keeps a hand-written `manifest` and **the
32	  gate enforces manifest ⇄ disk equality** — an unregistered case file never runs, so unregistered
33	  must be red.
34	
35	## 2. What the coverage gate checks
36	
37	The bijection gate is one committed test. It must fail on every one of: a leaf no case claims
38	(doc-first red-by-default); a case claiming a non-existent leaf; two cases claiming one leaf; a misnamed case file; a kind directory absent from the registry (or a
39	registered kind with no directory); a manifest out of sync with disk (where manifests exist); an
40	image found in a coded kind's folder (a screenshot cannot verify a gesture or a pure rule); a
41	stray golden no case or step accounts for. Every rule iterates the registry — adding a kind never
42	edits the gate.
43	
44	The gate checks repo state; an interactive feature run also has an *ordering*: after the
45	owner's feature-classified comment, an independent commit updating the spec (no code alongside)
46	precedes the first code commit on the branch. The spec's path defaults to the canonical
47	`dev/requirements/requirements.md`; a project whose spec lives elsewhere (a non-canonical
48	layout, or the pack pulled in via a `requires` from `spec-driven-product`) names it on the pack
49	entry as `config.spec`.
50	
51	## 3. The kind vocabulary
52	
53	Two forces pick a leaf's kind: what can **honestly observe** the assertion, and what gives the
54	**owner the simplest verification**. Prefer the kind whose expected is a **visual the owner checks
55	by sight** — a surface snapshot or a saga storyboard — and whose per-leaf test body is minimal:
56	drive to the state, capture, done, with the golden as the assertion rather than hand-written
57	expectations. Push as many requirements as can honestly be seen onto that visual path — the more
58	of the spec an owner verifies by *looking*, the more of it they actually review. Reserve the coded
59	kinds (behavior, logic) for what an image genuinely cannot see: a gesture's outgoing request, a
60	pure rule. Route each leaf to the kind that can actually see what it asserts:
61	
62	- **surface snapshot** (`popup`, `icon`, `screen`, …): a rendered resting state, pixel-exact
63	  against a committed golden. One golden per leaf, even when several leaves render the same state
64	  — the bijection stays strict.
65	- **behavior**: a driven gesture and its outgoing request/consequence, asserted in code against
66	  the fakes' recordings. No images allowed in the folder.
67	- **logic**: a pure product rule, a coded `verify()` importing shipped code.
68	- **saga** (§4): a multi-step story as a golden storyboard.
69	- **per-project kinds** where the product's value is breadth or crosses tiers: a per-target
70	  `extractor`/`support` kind (one case per supported external target, proven on committed real
71	  samples), a `server` kind (the boundary's half of a two-tier rule, against the real handler).
72	- **heavy/e2e singleton**: "the product loads in the real environment" — one case, its own lane,
73	  never in the default loop.
74	
75	## 4. Sagas: stories as storyboards
76	
77	Single frames prove states; **sagas prove transitions and causality** — what arriving, acting, or
78	time passing *changes*. Use a saga when the requirement is the story ("a message sent before I
79	arrived never appears; one sent after I arrived does"), not decomposable into independent resting
80	states without losing the claim.
81	
82	- A saga case is an ordered list of **steps**; each step = a caption plus an action against the
83	  fake world; after each step the runner captures one golden frame `<slug>.<id>.step-NN.png`.
84	- The **caption narrates the story** in user terms — captions surface in the gallery.
85	- One saga = one leaf; the frames are that one case's expected (all frames pixel-exact, same
86	  ownership rules as any golden). Keep sagas to 3–6 frames; a longer story is usually two sagas.
87	- Saga steps drive the **same real entry point** as every other kind (the shipped app shell/render
88	  function) — a saga must never become a scripted slideshow of hand-arranged states.
89	
90	**Animated saga goldens** (recording the motion, not the frames). A per-step frame proves a resting
91	state; a saga can instead be **one animated golden** — an APNG per leaf — recording the real UI
92	*moving* between steps. What keeps it delay-free and deterministic:
93	
94	- **Strip dead delay, keep the animation.** Render time is virtual, so a scripted wait is a run of
95	  *identical* frames — dedup consecutive identical frames and clamp any single hold, so the golden
96	  holds motion, never waiting (a 3 s wait must not become 3 s of golden).
97	- **Lossless, so byte-identity still holds.** Encode APNG, not GIF (whose palette and dithering
98	  aren't deterministic); the comparison stays exact byte-identity and a mismatch writes a per-frame
99	  `expected | actual | diff` to the gitignored failures dir. Capture at a low DPR — lossless costs
100	  no fidelity for it. Flutter reads each frame off the `RepaintBoundary` via `toImage` inside
101	  `runAsync` (the fake-async test zone won't otherwise complete the byte read).
102	- **Mark the gesture.** Paint an expanding ring at each real pointer gesture over the pre-reaction
103	  frame so the strip shows *where* the user acted; programmatic world changes draw none.
104	
105	## 5. Determinism or it isn't spec
106	
107	A rendered expected is only owner-ownable if it is byte-stable forever:
108	
109	- **Pin the clock.** One shared reference time (`REFERENCE_NOW`) threaded to everything that
110	  formats or compares dates; fixture data is authored relative to it. Never wall-clock.
111	- **Fake every nondeterministic input**: network (map tiles, avatars — deterministic generated
112	  substitutes), randomness, platform sensors, locale (pin it; date copy is locale-sensitive),
113	  viewport (one fixed logical size and pixel ratio).
114	- **Load real fonts** in the render harness — test environments default to a glyph-less stub that
115	  renders text as boxes. Load the product's bundled families plus the
116	  icon font; watch for styles that don't inherit the family (button text styles are the classic
117	  leak) — pin the family there explicitly.
118	- **Never wait for "settled".** Indeterminate spinners animate forever; use fixed-duration pumps
119	  so an in-flight state is a capturable, deterministic frame.
120	
121	## 6. Rendering recipes per stack
122	
123	- **Browser-extension / DOM products** (the origin recipe): feed the case's fake data to the real
124	  `render()` in a jsdom document seeded from the real HTML, fold the real CSS on as inline styles,
125	  rasterize with satori + resvg, compare with pixelmatch at **zero tolerated diff ratio**. No real
126	  browser: deterministic and dependency-light, at a documented fidelity tradeoff.
127	- **Flutter**: widget-test golden files are the native equivalent — pump the real app shell
128	  against the fake world and `matchesGoldenFile`; `--update-goldens` is the refresh lane. Load
129	  fonts from the FontManifest (icons included). The fake world (scripted location/auth/backend
130	  that also *records* what the UI asked) is the product's own testing library so the requirements
131	  package and unit tests share it.
132	- Whatever the stack: the comparison is **pixel-exact**. A tolerance is a standing invitation for
133	  unreviewed drift; if a platform renders unstably, fix the determinism (fonts, clock, fakes), not
134	  the threshold.
135	
136	## 7. The gallery is derived output
137	
138	- The spec doubles as a visual gallery: under every image-kind leaf, machine-managed image lines
139	  (tagged with an HTML comment marker) embed the committed goldens — saga leaves get their full
140	  captioned storyboard strip.
141	- A committed **gallery gate** keeps the doc equal to the generator's output byte-for-byte.
142	  Regenerate via the tool, never by hand.
143	
144	## 8. Refresh is a review step
145	
146	One committed refresh entry point regenerates all goldens **and** the gallery together, so they
147	cannot skew. Running it is how an *intended* UI change lands — the refreshed PNGs ride the diff
148	for the owner to approve. It is never how a red case gets fixed: the re-baselining approval
149	procedure (surface actual/expected/diff, ask, only then re-baseline) is canon in the
150	writing-tests skill and the spec-driven-product playbook.
151

1 # HTML 2 3 Portable, project-agnostic practices for hand-authored HTML — semantic markup, accessibility, forms, and the document structure pitfalls that recur regardless of framework — true for any HTML read cold. 4 5 - **Injected block markup inside a `

` silently empties it — read the sibling, not the tag.** When a `

` is filled with raw HTML (e.g. `innerHTML`, or a framework's `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` / `v-html` / `ng-bind-html`), a block element inside it (a `

`, etc.) is disallowed by the HTML content model, so the parser (browser or jsdom, same rule) auto-closes the `

` right before it and the injected content lands as the `

`'s **next sibling**. Read `element.nextElementSibling`. 6 - **An ambiguous numeric slash date can't be resolved from its digits — infer the document's convention once, don't guess per-field.** When both parts are ≤ 12 (e.g. `05/07/2026`), resolve the order once per document — never per source or per field — in this order. (1) **An unambiguous sibling date fixes the page's convention**: a slash date elsewhere on the same page with a part > 12 (e.g. `24/07/2026`) parses only one way, and a page is almost always internally consistent — read that date's order and apply it to every other slash date on the page. (2) Failing that, **read the declared locale** (``, `og:locale`): default **month-first** (the order `Date` and most JS parsers assume) and flip to day-first only on a *positive* non-US signal — a non-US region in `lang` / `og:locale`, or a non-English language; a bare `en` with unknown region stays month-first. The `.` / `-` separators are day-first regardless. 7 - **When code must react to how a real page actually behaves, investigate it live before you ship — don't deploy a hypothesis you can only test after release.** If a change hinges on the real DOM, computed styles, or runtime state of a page you can't see, hand the user one JavaScript snippet to run in the browser DevTools console and read its output back. Reserve "test it after it's deployed" for behavior you've verified genuinely can't be observed now. 8 - **Make that console request a snippet, not an essay.** Send exactly one code block to paste into the console and ask the user to paste its output back. Skip the prose explaining what you're hoping to learn. 9

1	# Leaflet
2	
3	Portable, project-agnostic gotchas for the [Leaflet](https://leafletjs.com/) web-mapping library — loading it from a CDN, embedding a map in a page, and the marker/`divIcon` and plugin behaviours that bite regardless of which app renders the map. True for any Leaflet map read cold.
4	
5	- **Feature-detect an optional Leaflet plugin before using it, and fall back to core when its CDN script didn't load.** A plugin's separate `<script>` (markercluster, heat, draw, …) can silently fail to load while the base Leaflet bundle succeeds, leaving `L.markerClusterGroup` (etc.) undefined. Guard the call with `typeof L.markerClusterGroup === "function"` and add markers straight to the map when it's absent — the base map must still render.
6	
7	- **Default an embedded, mid-page map to `scrollWheelZoom: false` so it doesn't hijack the page scroll.** Construct it with `L.map(el, { scrollWheelZoom: false })`, or gate wheel-zoom behind a click/focus.
8	
9	- **Keep the tile provider's attribution — it's a licence term, not decoration.** The `attribution: '… © OpenStreetMap contributors'` on the `L.tileLayer(...)` must stay even when tidying the UI. Set `maxZoom` to the provider's real ceiling (OSM tiles top out at 19) so Leaflet doesn't request zoom levels the provider doesn't serve.
10	
11	- **When a marker needs its own CSS `transform`, put it on an inner element, not the `divIcon` root.** Leaflet positions every marker by writing an inline `transform: translate3d(...)` onto the icon's root element, clobbering any `transform` you set there on the next reposition. Make the icon root a zero-size anchor (`iconSize: [0, 0]`, `iconAnchor: [0, 0]`) and apply your rotation/centring transform to a `<span>` inside its `html`.
12

1	# macOS
2	
3	Portable practices for a **native macOS app** — the ones that are true whatever the app does:
4	assembling the app bundle, the TCC and Hardened Runtime pair, the Developer ID → notarization →
5	DMG lane, and the process-lifecycle facts a Mac app cannot get wrong. A default to adapt, not a
6	contract.
7	
8	Distilled from a fleet project shipping a menu-bar agent app built with SwiftPM and published as a
9	notarized DMG. Mac App Store submission is a different track — see `app-store-release`; an iPhone
10	target is `ios`.
11	
12	## The app bundle is assembled, not built
13	
14	- **SwiftPM builds a binary; nothing builds you a `.app`.** `swift build -c release` yields an
15	  executable — the bundle (`Contents/MacOS/<exe>`, `Contents/Info.plist`,
16	  `Contents/Resources/`) is assembled by your own script. Keep that script the single place the
17	  bundle's shape is defined, so the local build and CI produce byte-identical layouts.
18	- **Commit one high-resolution icon master and generate the `.icns`** in the build script (`sips`
19	  to each size into an `.iconset`, then `iconutil -c icns`). Both tools ship with macOS, so the
20	  repo carries one PNG instead of ten, and the icon can't half-update.
21	- **A menu-bar-only app is `LSUIElement: true`** in `Info.plist` — that, not code, is what removes
22	  the Dock icon and the main window.
23	- **Pin `LSMinimumSystemVersion` to the same OS version the package's `platforms:` declares.** They
24	  are two independent claims about the same floor, and only one of them is enforced at launch.
25	
26	## TCC and the Hardened Runtime are two different gates — know which applies
27	
28	Every protected resource needs a **usage-description string** in `Info.plist` (the text of the
29	consent prompt; without it the app is killed rather than prompted) — one key per resource, and they
30	are separate keys for capabilities that feel like one feature: `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` covers
31	audio input, `NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription` covers the Speech framework, and an app that
32	listens *and* transcribes needs both or is killed at whichever it forgot. What each string says is
33	what the user consents to. Only *some* resources also need a **codesign entitlement**, and only
34	under the Hardened Runtime:
35	
36	- **Notarization requires the Hardened Runtime** (`codesign --options runtime`), and under it a
37	  resource-access exception must be granted explicitly by entitlement — device capture
38	  (`com.apple.security.device.audio-input`, camera) is the classic one. So **turning on
39	  notarization can silently break a capability an ad-hoc build had**, because the ad-hoc build was
40	  never running under the restriction. Ship the entitlement in the same change as the runtime flag.
41	- **Capabilities gated purely by TCC plus their usage string need no entitlement at all** (speech
42	  recognition is the worked example). Adding one you don't need is noise; omitting one you do need
43	  is a runtime failure no build step catches.
44	- **Do not enable the App Sandbox on the Developer ID track.** The sandbox belongs to the Mac App
45	  Store lane, needs a different (Apple Distribution) certificate, and silently removes
46	  capabilities the direct-download build has — distributed notifications, for one.
47	
48	## Speech recognition leaves the machine unless you say it must not
49	
50	- **`SFSpeechRecognizer` streams audio to Apple's servers by default.** On-device recognition is
51	  opt-in, and the opt-in is a property of the **request**
52	  (`request.requiresOnDeviceRecognition = true`), not of the recognizer — so it has to be set on
53	  every request the app builds, and a new call site added later starts out server-side. Nothing in
54	  the build says which mode ran; the difference is only visible in what left the machine.
55	- **The opt-in is only honourable where the locale's model is installed.** `supportsOnDeviceRecognition`
56	  is per-recognizer and false until then, and requiring on-device recognition where it isn't
57	  supported fails the request rather than quietly falling back — so check it and decide the degrade
58	  deliberately (refuse the feature, or say plainly that this locale would transcribe off-device).
59	- Speech is TCC-gated, so it needs its usage string and **no** entitlement — see the section above.
60	
61	## Keep signing and notarization an optional, secret-gated lane
62	
63	- **The unsigned path must stay a working path.** Gate the Developer ID + notarization steps on the
64	  signing secrets being present, and ship an **ad-hoc-signed** artifact when they aren't. Make
65	  signing a required step and every fork, and every build in a repo whose secrets aren't set, goes
66	  red for a reason unrelated to the change.
67	- **An ad-hoc signature cannot be notarized.** They are separate lanes, not degrees of the same
68	  one: only an identity-signed bundle can be submitted to the notary service. Don't write a
69	  pipeline that "tries" to notarize whatever it just signed.
70	- **Notarize the distributed container, then staple it** (`notarytool submit --wait`, then `stapler
71	  staple` and `stapler validate`). Stapling is what makes the download open offline without a
72	  round-trip to Apple; skipping it works on your machine and fails on a user's.
73	- **In CI, an imported identity must be in the searchable keychain list.** Creating an ephemeral
74	  keychain, importing the `.p12` and setting the key partition list is not enough —
75	  `codesign` searches the *user's keychain list*, so the new keychain has to be added to it or the
76	  identity is simply not found.
77	- **Say out loud, in a build annotation, which lane ran.** "No signing secret — publishing an
78	  ad-hoc build" turns a silently-degraded artifact into a visible one.
79	
80	## Distribution and the Gatekeeper story you owe the user
81	
82	- **A drag-to-install DMG is a staged folder, not Finder scripting.** Stage the `.app` beside a
83	  symlink to `/Applications`, drop the icon in as `.VolumeIcon.icns`, flag the folder as having a
84	  custom icon, and let `hdiutil create` carry it through. Anything that automates Finder to lay out
85	  the window is fragile in CI and unnecessary.
86	- **Write the Gatekeeper bypass for the OS your users are on.** macOS 15 removed the
87	  right-click → *Open* bypass; the current path is System Settings → Privacy & Security →
88	  *Open Anyway*, or `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine <app>`. An install doc that still says
89	  right-click → Open reads as broken software.
90	- **A notarized build should need none of that** — if your README's manual-bypass section is the
91	  one users actually follow, the signing lane isn't running.
92	
93	## Assume the user's Mac has no developer toolchain
94	
95	The machine running a distributed app installed the artifact; it has no Xcode. Two consequences:
96	
97	- **Diagnostics belong inside the shipped app**, or in a script using only what ships with macOS.
98	  Anything requiring a compiler on the user's machine is a diagnostic that will never be run.
99	- **`command -v swift` does not test for a Swift toolchain.** `/usr/bin/swift` exists on every Mac
100	  as a stub that pops the *"install the command line developer tools?"* dialog when invoked — so
101	  the probe passes and the script asks the user to install several gigabytes of Xcode. Gate on
102	  `xcode-select -p >/dev/null 2>&1`, which fails quietly when the tools are absent.
103	
104	## Exit paths: `applicationWillTerminate` is not "every exit"
105	
106	- **`NSApplication` installs no signal handlers.** `NSApp.terminate` (menu Quit, ⌘Q, the
107	  logout/shutdown Apple Event) runs `applicationWillTerminate`; a bare `SIGTERM` (Activity
108	  Monitor's Quit, `killall`), `SIGINT` or `SIGHUP` kills the process with **no** teardown. Route
109	  them through a `DispatchSourceSignal` into `NSApp.terminate` — and set `signal(sig, SIG_IGN)`
110	  **before** `resume()`, or a signal arriving in the gap still takes the fatal default.
111	  `SIGKILL`, Force Quit and a crash stay uncoverable; name that as residual risk rather than
112	  claiming coverage.
113	- **An uncaught Objective-C exception is an exit path too.** It aborts the process, so no teardown
114	  runs; a framework call that *raises* (rather than throws) is therefore a resource-release bug as
115	  well as a crash. Swift cannot catch `NSException` — a tiny Objective-C target of your own is the
116	  only trap, and it is only safe around calls that validate before mutating.
117	
118	## Sleep, wake, and deferred work
119	
120	- **There is no "the machine is back" notification.** `NSWorkspace.didWakeNotification` also fires
121	  for a dark/Power-Nap wake with nobody there. Fan in the several signals that a real return emits
122	  (wake, screens wake, session became active, the screen-unlocked distributed notification) and
123	  **coalesce them** — a genuine return fires a burst, and each must not schedule its own work.
124	- **Coalesce with an id, not a boolean.** A single `pending` flag deadlocks: something invalidates
125	  the timer, the timer clears the flag, and whichever ordering loses leaves the next wake either
126	  unable to schedule or double-scheduling. Hold the in-flight work's id; a stale timer compares its
127	  captured id and returns.
128	- **`asyncAfter` work scheduled before sleep fires immediately on wake.** Give every intentional
129	  stop a generation counter, capture the generation when scheduling, and abort in the closure if it
130	  moved — otherwise deferred work reacquires resources on the way *into* sleep or before the
131	  machine has settled. When cancelling in-flight work, reset the latches beside it too, or they
132	  stay stuck and block everything after.
133	- **Measure a span that includes a sleep with `Date()`, not `ProcessInfo.systemUptime`.** The
134	  monotonic clock does not advance while the machine sleeps — which is exactly the span you are
135	  trying to measure. Use `systemUptime` for the opposite question ("how long, while we were
136	  awake").
137	
138	## Holding a device the user can unplug
139	
140	If the app captures from shared hardware (microphone, camera), these are the rules that cost the
141	most to learn:
142	
143	- **Release the device on every path where capture ends.** A process that dies with its IO proc
144	  still registered can leave some USB devices wedged until physically re-plugged. This is necessary
145	  and *not sufficient* — a device can also wedge below the user-space audio daemon, where no
146	  teardown of yours helps.
147	- **Never construct a capture engine to ask whether a device exists.** Materializing an input node
148	  opens the default device and mints a hidden per-client aggregate device; a retry ladder built on
149	  that is not a cheap probe but an open/close plus an aggregate create-and-destroy, repeated for as
150	  long as the hardware is missing. Query the HAL's device properties instead — a property read
151	  opens nothing and can be sampled forever for free. The churn is observable rather than
152	  theoretical: each hidden aggregate appears in the HAL as `CADefaultDeviceAggregate-<pid>-<n>`, so
153	  what a retry ladder is really doing can be counted instead of argued about.
154	- **Presence is not usability, at either layer.** Mid-teardown a device enumerates as alive with an
155	  unreadable name and a **zero** sample rate. Require a nonzero rate and a sane channel count, and
156	  judge the *system default* input — a healthy device behind a broken default is not one you can
157	  capture from. One layer up, the engine lies in the opposite direction: with the input torn down,
158	  the input node's `outputFormat(forBus: 0)` still reports a plausible 48 kHz while its
159	  `inputFormat` reports 0, so a guard written against the wrong one waves through starts that
160	  cannot succeed — read both and require them to agree. Whatever a new probe reads, ask what that
161	  field says while the device is absent.
162	- **A duration is a claim about a span you observed.** "It has been present for N seconds" is only
163	  as good as the observation behind it: a state maintained by a timer must be **seeded at start**
164	  (a repeating timer does not fire immediately) and **invalidated across any gap** — a sleep is a
165	  gap, and carrying a settle clock straight through one makes the gate inert on exactly the
166	  transition it was built for. Model "not observed" as its own state, distinct from "absent", and
167	  key the span on the device's **UID** — an unplug-and-replug, or a swap for a different mic, is a
168	  new arrival that starts its own clock rather than inheriting the departed device's.
169	- **"Started" is not "working".** A running engine delivering buffers of pure silence looks
170	  identical to a healthy one from the inside. Measure what actually arrives, publish a health state
171	  the UI renders, and when a failure mode has exactly one remedy, name **that** remedy rather than
172	  the generic one.
173	- **Compile-green is not a gate for device code.** `swift build` cannot see a raise-vs-throw bug or
174	  a lifecycle race, and both are reachable in the first second of a run. A change here is not
175	  verified until the app has actually launched on a Mac. Reaching the interesting case needs no
176	  hardware theatre: let the display sleep and `coreaudiod` tears its device contexts down seconds
177	  later, which is the same transition as an unplug from the app's point of view.
178

1	# Node.js
2	
3	Portable, project-agnostic practices for working in Node.js / npm codebases — package management, scripts, module resolution, runtime gotchas — true for any Node project read cold.
4	
5	## Module resolution
6	
7	- **A *named* import from a package's CommonJS entry can silently yield `undefined`.** Node recovers named bindings from a CJS module by static analysis, and that analysis fails on plenty of real entry points (a re-export built at runtime, a conditional assignment) — with no error: the import resolves, the binding is `undefined`, and the failure surfaces later as "x is not a function". When a package ships both entries, import the **ESM** one explicitly (`…/package/index.mjs`, or the `import` condition of its `exports`) for named bindings; when it doesn't, `import pkg from '…'` and destructure off the default. Resolve the package's own directory (`$(npm root -g)/<pkg>` for a global install) rather than hardcoding an absolute path into a version-pinned layout, which moves under you on the next image or upgrade.
8	- **Modern Node (22.7+) detects ES-module syntax in a `.js` file on its own** — no `"type": "module"`, no flag, no warning. A directory of ES modules therefore needs **no `package.json` of its own** just to be loadable; adding one to declare module-ness is cargo cult, and one already present for that reason is vestigial. (Prefer `.js` consistently within a tree over mixing in `.mjs` for the same purpose; the extension is then a style choice, not a signal.)
9	
10	## Test discovery
11	
12	- **`node --test` skips dot-directories, so a bare invocation over a suite living under one runs
13	  zero tests and exits green.** Node's default discovery walks the tree but ignores hidden
14	  directories outright, and finding nothing is *success* — a run reporting no failures because it
15	  found no tests reads exactly like a passing suite. Any CI step or local command meant to exercise
16	  tests under a dot-path must pass that path (or an explicit glob) as an argument, and whoever adds
17	  the step confirms it by watching the **test count be non-zero**, never by watching it go green.
18	  Naming a path is not enough — the argument must **resolve to files that exist**: a typo'd
19	  glob, a moved fixture or a renamed directory produces the identical zero-test green, so the
20	  property to assert is that every path a `node --test` invocation names still matches something
21	  in the tree.
22	
23	## jsdom diverges from a real browser in ways a green test can hide
24	
25	Two that recur:
26	
27	- **`body.innerText` is null in jsdom.** Code reading `el.innerText || el.textContent` therefore falls through to `textContent` under test, which *includes* the `<script>` / `<style>` text, `<select>` / `<option>` text, and CSS-hidden text a real browser's `innerText` omits. Treat body-text results as jsdom-optimistic; never add a test that only passes because of it.
28	- **`runScripts: "outside-only"` (the default) parses `<noscript>` into live DOM — the opposite of a real browser.** A `textContent` read looks clean under test but splices the `<noscript>` markup into the value in Chrome, which keeps `<noscript>` as raw text. Parse a script-free fragment with `runScripts: "dangerously"` to reproduce the browser.
29

1	# Python
2	
3	Portable, project-agnostic practices for a Python package built around an optional
4	heavy/native dependency (an ML model, a native audio/GPU library, a cloud SDK) that
5	most of the codebase — and the whole test suite — must run without. The theme is one:
6	**keep the importable core dependency-free, and gate every heavy thing behind an
7	optional extra.** What stays here is the architecture judgment that has no
8	false-positive-free static signature; the mechanical shape of the optional import
9	itself (imported lazily, guarded with an install-hint re-raise) is carried by the
10	`python-optional-deps` skill.
11	
12	## Keep the importable core dependency-free; heavy/native deps go in optional extras, not base `dependencies`
13	
14	The core of a package (its logic, storage, CLI, any web/dashboard layer) should import
15	and run — and be **fully testable** — with only the Python standard library. Declare
16	`dependencies = []` (or the genuinely-always-needed minimum) in `[project]`, and put every
17	heavy, native, or ML dependency under a **named `[project.optional-dependencies]` extra**
18	(`pkg[yamnet]`, `pkg[speaker]`, `pkg[dev]`). The test: if a `pip install <pkg>` with no
19	extra can't import the core, a heavy dependency has leaked into the base set — move it
20	to an extra.
21	
22	## Provide a stdlib-only implementation behind the same interface so tests and offline modes need no extra
23	
24	Give the swappable interface a **dependency-free** implementation — a scripted/mock
25	backend built on the standard library alone — alongside the heavy real one; that stdlib
26	backend is what the test suite and any offline/`simulate` mode run on. The heavy backend
27	is then just one more implementation of the interface, selected at runtime, never a hard
28	import the core or the tests depend on. The clean shape is a tiny backend interface plus
29	a `load_default()`/registry that lazy-imports the *selected* backend by name, so the
30	module that wires backends together never imports any of them at load time.
31	
32	## Mark the availability-probe import as a deliberate unused-import suppression
33	
34	An import kept **only** to probe whether an optional stack is present (its name is never
35	used directly — the code just branches on whether the import succeeded) is a real linter
36	false-positive for unused-import (`F401`). Mark that line `# noqa: F401` and record the
37	deliberate suppression, rather than deleting the probe or letting the warning ride.
38

1	# product-wiki — the self-growing product research wiki
2	
3	This project keeps its market/user/competitor research as a self-growing wiki
4	under `product-wiki/` (Karpathy's LLM-wiki pattern: compile findings once, refine in
5	place). Layout, required page sections, the Key insights header's shape,
6	growth-log dating, source links, staleness, and the isolation wall are
7	**check-enforced** — the finding is the instruction, so this prose never restates
8	them. The full growth procedure is the pack's task doc
9	(`packs/product-wiki/tasks/wiki-growth/task.md`).
10	
11	- **Every page opens with what it found.** `## Key insights` leads the page: a
12	  few bullets carrying the research's actual conclusions — the numbers, the
13	  competitor that already does this, the thing that turned out not to be true —
14	  enough that a human who reads only the header understands what was researched
15	  and what it means. Not a table of contents ("covers pricing and competitors"),
16	  not a teaser. The body is where the reader goes for evidence, nuance and
17	  citations; the header is where they decide whether they need to.
18	- **Terse, plain, and only the non-obvious.** One short line per bullet, in
19	  ordinary words — no qualifying clause, no citation, no hedge, no jargon a
20	  newcomer would have to decode. Prefer the finding that would *surprise*
21	  someone who knows the field: the thing that turned out not to be true, the
22	  number nobody expects, the competitor who already shipped it. Whether a point
23	  is obvious is genuinely hard to call, so **don't agonise — when in doubt, keep
24	  it**. A borderline-obvious line costs the reader two seconds; a long, careful
25	  line costs them the header.
26	- **The header is a current view, not a log.** A pass that changes what a page's
27	  most important findings are rewrites the header to match — a superseded
28	  insight leaves it (the correction and its why stay in the body, per below),
29	  and an insight the pass didn't touch stays put. If nothing changed the page's
30	  top-line understanding, the header doesn't move.
31	- **The sink is human-reviewed only.** `product-wiki/product-requirements/` never
32	  changes as a side effect of wiki work or any unattended pass — a wiki finding
33	  that should move a requirement gets a growth-log note (and a repo issue) and
34	  waits for a human. It is the only `product-wiki/` content the rest of the repo may
35	  build on.
36	- **Compile once, refine in place.** Read the target page end to end before
37	  researching; `## Open questions` is the backlog — research what it flags as
38	  open, thin, or dated, and spot-check an existing citation or two per pass.
39	  Never re-derive a claim that's already cited and current.
40	- **Cited, never silently rewritten.** An uncited claim doesn't get written. A
41	  wrong or superseded claim is corrected with a note of why (and its source),
42	  never deleted without trace. Every real change records itself in the page's
43	  growth log and updates the open questions in both directions.
44	- **Seeing a figure in several places is not evidence of who published it.**
45	  Search snippets quote each other, so a number that recurs across five results
46	  is one source repeated, and the firm the snippets name is routinely not the
47	  firm that produced it. When you cannot open the report, attribute the figure to
48	  the publisher a source explicitly names as its **origin**; when sources
49	  disagree about that, say so on the page rather than picking one.
50	- **No fabricated growth.** Most passes find little or nothing; no new citable
51	  material → no edit, no log entry, no PR.
52	- **sample-data and new wikis.** `product-wiki/sample-data/` gains a file only when
53	  a wiki claim needs one to point to — never test fixtures (anything a test
54	  asserts against belongs in engineering's tree). Any folder under `product-wiki/`
55	  outside the two reserved names *is* a wiki (the structural classifier), so
56	  create one only deliberately, seeded with its required sections; automation
57	  refines existing pages, it never invents new ones.
58	- **Review discipline.** Unattended growth always lands as an unmerged PR —
59	  researched claims entering a committed knowledge base need the review gate.
60	  The owner phrase **"grow the product wiki"** runs the worker method
61	  in-session with full web tooling: same rules, same PR discipline.
62

# Revalidatable Claims by File

## 1. packs/chrome-extension/skills/chrome-store-releases/SKILL.md

- "GitHub only resolves a reusable workflow or composite action from a repo's own `.github/`" — probe: whether GitHub Actions can resolve a reusable workflow/composite action from another repo (cross-repo `uses:` references), which would undercut the "must vendor" premise.
- "`https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/latest/download/<zip>` … a permanent newest-build URL" — probe: GitHub Releases' `/releases/latest/download/<asset>` URL semantics still resolve to the latest release's matching asset.
- "Release + publish are invoked via `workflow_call` because a `GITHUB_TOKEN` push triggers no workflows." — probe: whether a push authored with the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` still fails to trigger `on: push` workflows.
- "`chrome-webstore-upload-cli@3` … reads env `EXTENSION_ID` / `CLIENT_ID` / `CLIENT_SECRET` / `REFRESH_TOKEN`" — probe: current major version's CLI flags and required env var names.
- "While the item is **pending review the API rejects uploads**" — probe: Chrome Web Store publish API behavior during `ITEM_PENDING_REVIEW`.
- "Every subsequent upload must carry a **strictly higher** version" — probe: Chrome Web Store's version-monotonicity requirement on upload.
- "approval takes hours to a few days (`ITEM_PENDING_REVIEW` = success)" — probe: current review turnaround and status-code semantics.
- "will hit a **'Google hasn't verified this app'** interstitial … an unverified app's tokens work indefinitely" — probe: Google OAuth consent-screen behavior for unverified apps and whether unverified-app tokens still function without expiry.
- "Left in 'Testing', refresh tokens silently expire after 7 days" — probe: Google OAuth testing-mode refresh-token expiry policy.
- "type **Web application** (NOT Desktop — Desktop clients can't take custom redirect URIs …)" — probe: Google OAuth client-type restrictions on custom redirect URIs.
- "add authorized redirect URI exactly `https://developers.google.com/oauthplayground`" — probe: OAuth Playground's current required redirect URI.
- "Ignore the access token — it expires hourly" — probe: Google OAuth access-token lifetime.
- "`npx chrome-webstore-upload-keys` … it needs the client to be a **Desktop app**, whose `http://localhost` redirect it uses" — probe: this package's current auth flow/client-type requirement.
- "Once the store approves, Chrome auto-pushes the update to installed users within hours — no reinstall." — probe: Chrome's extension auto-update propagation behavior/timing.
- "HTTP 400 `Publish condition not met: Privacy policy link is not reachable.`" — probe: exact error text/code the Chrome Web Store API currently returns for an unreachable privacy URL.
- "Google fetches the listing's privacy-policy URL at publish time, and re-checks it on **every** publish." — probe: whether Chrome Web Store still re-validates the privacy URL on every publish.
- "Register a developer account … (one-time $5 fee)" — probe: current Chrome Web Store developer registration fee.
- "the store assigns the ID at first upload" — probe: Chrome Web Store item-ID assignment behavior on first upload (and that a `key` must be absent on that first upload).
- "A new **required** permission that carries an install-time warning disables the extension for existing users until each one re-approves it" — probe: Chrome's current behavior for required-permission changes on existing installs.
- "the store blocks publishing the new version until it does" (permission justification) — probe: whether the dashboard's Privacy-practices requirement still gates publish.

## 2. packs/claude-code-web-users-support/RULES.md

- "A Claude Code **web** session runs for a signed-in person, in a managed container. A terminal session does neither." — probe: whether Claude Code web sessions still run in a managed container tied to signed-in identity, distinct from terminal sessions.
- "Only a managed container has a **Setup script** field, and the web base image ships no toolchains" — probe: current Claude Code web environment's Setup-script feature and base-image toolchain contents.
- "it becomes a case-sensitive `raw.githubusercontent.com` path segment that a local checkout would happily serve either way" — probe: whether `raw.githubusercontent.com` path lookups remain case-sensitive.

## 3. packs/claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/RULES.md

No revalidatable claims found — content is entirely about this pack's own sweep policy, config, and internal fleet mechanics (repo-organization/process judgment, out of scope).

## 4. packs/claudinite-growth/skills/extract-from-activity/SKILL.md

No revalidatable claims found — pure process/judgment guidance about how to mine repo artifacts for lessons.

## 5. packs/claudinite-growth/skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md

## 7. packs/claudinite-growth/skills/growth-dedup/SKILL.md

## 8. packs/claudinite-growth/skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md

No revalidatable claims found — process/judgment guidance about converting prose to checks.

## 9. packs/claudinite-growth/skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md

- "a raw `api.github.com` `fetch`, or a `process.env.GITHUB_TOKEN` read in in-session code … will 401 in the MCP-only session it's scheduled in" — probe: whether an in-session (non-Actions) agent still lacks `GITHUB_TOKEN` and gets 401 on direct REST calls.
- "`curl` does — never a bare `node -e \"fetch(...)\"`, whose global `fetch` ignores `HTTPS_PROXY` and goes **direct**" — probe: whether Node's global `fetch` still ignores `HTTPS_PROXY` while `curl` still honors it in this sandbox.
- "the multi-agent-orchestration **Workflow tool** … mandates an interactive opt-in on *every* run (the prompt only disappears under bypass-permissions / headless modes …)" — probe: current Workflow tool's approval-prompt behavior and which modes suppress it.
- "Fan out with **plain subagent dispatch** (the Agent/Task tool) instead — it carries no such gate" — probe: whether Agent/Task subagent dispatch still requires no interactive approval.
- "Pass the isolation flag on the dispatch (`isolation: \"worktree\"`)" — probe: current dispatch API/parameter name for worktree isolation.
- "There is no platform wall-clock kill for a launched agent session" — probe: whether the platform (harness/Actions) still enforces no hard timeout on a launched agent session.
- "The GitHub toolsets these runs use offer comment *creation* and no comment-update tool" — probe: current GitHub MCP/tool surface for whether a comment-update tool exists.
- "An agent session also has **no ambient clock**: a timestamp is only true if you read it" — probe: whether agent sessions still lack ambient wall-clock awareness absent an explicit read.
- "the harness still flags the completion with a security warning because no human approval appears in the transcript" (`[Merge Without Review]`) — probe: whether the harness still emits this specific warning for unattended merges lacking human approval in transcript.
- "A background subagent dispatch shares the parent's working directory unless isolated" — probe: current default working-directory behavior for background subagent dispatch.
- "When a task needs several deferred/lazily-loaded tools (schemas fetched via a tool-search or discovery call rather than present from the start)" — probe: whether the harness's deferred-tool/ToolSearch mechanism still works this way.
- "CI success transitions are frequently not delivered as webhook events, so the green signal never arrives" — probe: current GitHub webhook delivery reliability for CI-success state transitions.
- "opening a PR on the same commit fires an identical second run" — probe: whether GitHub Actions still triggers a duplicate CI run when a PR is opened on an already-pushed commit.
- "The hook's stdout becomes context the agent reads — the runtime never intercepts it" (SessionStart hook) — probe: current Claude Code SessionStart hook mechanism — stdout injected as context vs. enforced by runtime.
- "An `@import` is expanded inline at launch in *every* session regardless of relevance" — probe: current CLAUDE.md `@import` expansion behavior at session launch.

## 10. packs/claudinite-growth/skills/writing-tasks/SKILL.md

No revalidatable claims found — the file describes Claudinite's own scheduler/task-engine architecture and conventions (self-referential system design, explicitly out of scope as "how this repo itself is organized"), not external harness/GitHub/MCP behavior.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about GitHub Actions scheduled workflows being automatically disabled:

## Key Finding

In a public repository, scheduled workflows are automatically disabled when no repository activity has occurred in 60 days. The 60-day auto-disable policy applies to both public and private repositories.

## Important Details

Only new commits reset the inactivity timer. Other repository events such as creating releases, pushing tags, opening issues, or merging pull requests do not count as qualifying activity and will not prevent the scheduled workflows from being disabled.

When a public repository is forked, scheduled workflows are disabled by default.

## Workarounds

There are several approaches to prevent this automatic disabling:

1. **Keepalive Actions**: The open-source actions/gh-action-keepalive and Keepalive Workflow action on the GitHub Marketplace both automate this. These automatically generate git activity (commits) to reset the inactivity timer.

2. **Manual Re-enabling**: You can manually re-enable disabled workflows through the GitHub Actions interface, though this requires periodic maintenance.

This feature was implemented by GitHub to prevent unnecessary workflow runs on inactive projects, but it can catch users off guard if they're relying on scheduled workflows to run periodically.

Based on the search results, I found information about RFC 7518's HMAC key size requirement. A key of the same size as the hash output (for instance, 256 bits for "HS256") or larger MUST be used with this algorithm.

This requirement is based on Section 5.3.4 (Security Effect of the HMAC Key) of NIST SP 800-117 [NIST.800-107], which states that the effective security strength is the minimum of the security strength of the key and two times the size of the internal hash value.

The requirement for HMAC keys to be "at least equal to the size of the hash output" is a security best practice that ensures the cryptographic strength of the HMAC implementation is not undermined by weak key material.

Based on the search results, here's what I found:

In macOS Sequoia, users will no longer be able to Control-click to override Gatekeeper when opening software that isn't signed correctly or notarized. Instead of right-clicking, the process now involves venturing into the Privacy & Security section, hitting a button, confirming, and then entering your admin password to confirm again before you can open the blocked app.

This change aims to combat stealer malware and backdoors that often bypass Gatekeeper protections by being unsigned and tricking users into granting them access.

More specifically, macOS 15 removed control-click > Open as a mechanism to bypass Gatekeeper. Additionally, with version 15.1 disabling ways to bypass this completely.

The new process requires users to access System Settings > Privacy & Security to manually approve unsigned applications, making it more difficult for users to inadvertently grant permission to potentially malicious software through simple right-click shortcuts.

# basics pack

The baseline pack — the `RULES.md` prose every session loads (injected by the pack-prose hook) plus the working-discipline checks. Its subject is **how work is done**, whatever tool is running it. content.content:
1	// The machine-readable records a task's execution leaves in an Actions log
2	// (skill-usage-metrics DESIGN §4.2), and the parsers that read them back.
3	//
4	// TWO FAMILIES, ONE OF THEM HISTORICAL. `claudinite-task-run` was the SLOT
5	// scheduler's own line, one per due task per run; the slot scheduler is retired
6	// (#974) and nothing writes that line any more. The parser stays, and only the
7	// parser: Actions logs from before the retirement are still inside their retention
8	// window, and the usage fold still counts them. Nothing new should be taught this
9	// shape — `claudinite-task-exec` below is the live record.
10	//
11	// The counts these produce are exact within the Actions log retention window, and
12	// that is worth stating next to the capture-derived counts they land beside.
13	
14	// The five things a slot scheduler run could do with a due task. One name per
15	// outcome, used verbatim as the counter key in the aggregate, so there is no
16	// mapping table between "what the run said" and "what the fold counted" to drift.
17	export const TASK_RUN_OUTCOMES = Object.freeze([
18	  // A dispatch issue was filed: an agent session ran this task.
19	  'agent',
20	  // The task ran with NO agent — an `agent_model: none` task (code-work is the
21	  // whole task), or an agentful one whose code-work requested no agent phase.
22	  // Kebab, not the declaration field's `code_work`: this word is a WIRE token,
23	  // constrained to the line format's `[a-z-]+` charset.
24	  'code-work',
25	  // Due, but its precondition said there was nothing to do.
26	  'skipped',
27	  // Its code-work failed; the run converged the task to a needs-human issue.
28	  'failed',
29	  // Due and past its precondition, but no NEW agent run started: this slot was
30	  // already dispatched (exactly-once), an earlier dispatch is still open
31	  // (at-most-one-open), or another task claimed the run exclusively. Work that
32	  // was wanted and did not happen this run.
33	  'deferred',
34	]);
35	
36	// An empty per-task counter row — every outcome present, zeros included, so a row's
37	// shape never depends on which outcomes a task happened to hit.
38	export const emptyTaskRun = () => Object.fromEntries(TASK_RUN_OUTCOMES.map((o) => [o, 0]));
39	
40	// The line format. `v1` is the shape's version: a reader that meets a `v2` line
41	// knows it is looking at something it was not written for, instead of silently
42	// half-parsing it.
43	export const TASK_RUN_TAG = 'claudinite-task-run';
44	const VERSION = 'v1';
45	
46	// Actions stamps every log line with its own timestamp before the command's output,
47	// so the parse tolerates that prefix — without it, a fetched log reads as having
48	// printed nothing at all.
49	const LINE_RE = new RegExp(
50	  String.raw`^(?:\S+\s+)?${TASK_RUN_TAG} ${VERSION} (\S+)/(\S+) \[(\S+)\] ([a-z-]+)\s*$`,
51	);
52	
53	// One line → `{ pack, task, slotId, outcome }`, or null for anything that is not a
54	// record of this version. Deliberately strict: an unknown outcome word is NOT a
55	// record, because counting it would mint a counter key nothing ever reads.
56	// The code phase has been renamed twice, and job logs outlive both renames:
57	// `preprocess` (pre-2026-08-06) and `prework` (pre-2026-08-18) are the earlier
58	// words for what is now `code-work`. Runs logged under either still parse, each
59	// normalized straight to the canonical word.
60	// Exported because the outcome words are also the usage aggregate's counter KEYS,
61	// and that file holds rows written under the older words. Its decode renames them
62	// by this same map, so a rename never silently drops a historical count.
63	export const LEGACY_TASK_RUN_OUTCOMES = Object.freeze({ preprocess: 'code-work', prework: 'code-work' });
64	
65	export function parseTaskRun(line) {
66	  const m = LINE_RE.exec(line);
67	  if (!m) return null;
68	  const [, pack, task, slotId, word] = m;
69	  const outcome = LEGACY_TASK_RUN_OUTCOMES[word] ?? word;
70	  if (!TASK_RUN_OUTCOMES.includes(outcome)) return null;
71	  return { pack, task, slotId, outcome };
72	}
73	
74	// Every record in one job log. The log is the whole job's output — this picks its
75	// own lines out of it and ignores everything else.
76	export function parseTaskRuns(text) {
77	  const out = [];
78	  for (const line of String(text ?? '').split('\n')) {
79	    const rec = parseTaskRun(line);
80	    if (rec) out.push(rec);
81	  }
82	  return out;
83	}
84	
85	// --- executor-side execution records ------------------------------------------
86	// The historical records above say what the retired slot scheduler DID with a due
87	// task; these record what an EXECUTOR SESSION did with the work it ran. Printed by executor-side code
88	// (resolve-dispatch on a terminal verdict, record-exec.mjs at convergence), they
89	// land in the session transcript, ride to the conversation-logs branch with the
90	// executor's capture step, and the usage fold counts them deterministically —
91	// the "task statuses out of the conversation logs" half of the census (owner,
92	// 2026-08-06). Same single-home rule: renderer and parser sit here together.
93	
94	export const TASK_EXEC_STATUSES = Object.freeze([
95	  // The dispatch ran to completion within its ceiling; the issue was closed.
96	  'success',
97	  // The run failed (task failure or ceiling violation); converged to needs-human.
98	  'failed',
99	  // The dispatch named a task the repo no longer carries (file gone, pack
100	  // undeclared) — the executor closed the issue as obsolete. Not a failure.
101	  'task-gone',
102	  // The dispatch was malformed (bad path shape, unparseable declaration) and was
103	  // converged to needs-human without running.
104	  'invalid',
105	]);
106	
107	export const TASK_EXEC_TAG = 'claudinite-task-exec';
108	
109	// The bracketed field is the OCCURRENCE'S IDENTITY, which is a different thing under
110	// each dispatch mechanism: a slot id (`d2026-08-06`) where slots decide what runs, and
111	// the work item's issue number (`#867`) where the queue does. `slotId` keeps its name
112	// for the fielded records that already carry one; what it must never become is a
113	// constant, since it is the only join from a record back to the work it describes.
114	export const renderTaskExec = ({ pack, task, slotId, status }) =>
115	  `${TASK_EXEC_TAG} ${VERSION} ${pack}/${task} [${slotId ?? 'unknown'}] ${status}`;
116	
117	const EXEC_LINE_RE = new RegExp(
118	  String.raw`(?:^|\s)${TASK_EXEC_TAG} ${VERSION} (\S+)/(\S+) \[(\S+)\] ([a-z-]+)\s*$`,
119	);
120	
121	export function parseTaskExec(line) {
122	  const m = EXEC_LINE_RE.exec(line);
123	  if (!m) return null;
124	  const [, pack, task, slotId, status] = m;
125	  if (!TASK_EXEC_STATUSES.includes(status)) return null;
126	  return { pack, task, slotId, status };
127	}
128	
129	export function parseTaskExecs(text) {
